techniques.name: Mean Decrease Impurity
techniques.description: Mean Decrease Impurity (MDI) scores how much each feature contributes to a tree-based model, such as a random forest, by looking at how the model's decision trees split the training data. Each split sends cases into two groups, and a good split makes each group more uniform in its outcome, which is a drop in impurity, measured with a score such as Gini impurity. For each feature, MDI adds up the drops from every split that uses it, weights each by the share of training cases reaching that split, and averages over all trees. The scores are usually scaled to sum to one, so they show relative importance. Because they come from the training data, they describe how the model was built, not how well each feature predicts on new data.

example_use_cases.description: Determining the most influential genetic markers in a decision tree model predicting disease susceptibility, by identifying which markers consistently lead to the purest splits between healthy and diseased patient groups.

A model-validation team reviews a gradient-boosted loan-default model and ranks its inputs by MDI before sign-off. They investigate any identifier-like or many-valued field, such as customer ID or postcode, that ranks near the top, because MDI favours such fields and they may reflect overfitting rather than real predictive signal.

An environmental analytics team fits a random forest to forecast air quality and uses MDI to choose which weather stations' readings to drop from a simpler model. They then confirm on held-out data that accuracy holds, because MDI alone reflects the training data.

limitations.description: MDI favours features with many distinct values, because more possible split points give more chances of a good split by chance. Strobl and colleagues found that uninformative continuous or many-category variables were preferred over informative ones when predictors differed in type or number of categories.

Scores are calculated from the training data, so a feature can rank high because the model fitted noise in it. A high score does not show that the feature helps predictions on unseen data, and scikit-learn recommends permutation importance on held-out data as the alternative.

MDI gives only a non-negative score for each feature. It does not show whether higher values of a feature raise or lower the prediction, so it cannot support a claim about the direction of a feature's effect.

Scores vary from tree to tree, and the scikit-learn example plots this spread as error bars. A forest with few trees, or a small training set, can therefore give a ranking that shifts when the model is refitted.
Correlated predictors compete for splits. One can mask another's importance, and changing the fitted ensemble or candidate-feature settings can change their relative ranks.

resources.title: Random Forests
resources.abstract: Random forests are a combination of tree predictors such that each tree depends on the values of a random vector sampled independently and with the same distribution for all trees in the forest. The generalization error for forests converges a.s. to a limit as the number of trees in the forest becomes large. The generalization error of a forest of tree classifiers depends on the strength of the individual trees in the forest and the correlation between them. Using a random selection of features to split each node yields error rates that compare favorably to Adaboost (Y. Freund & R. Schapire, Machine Learning: Proceedings of the Thirteenth International conference, ***, 148–156), but are more robust with respect to noise. Internal estimates monitor error, strength, and correlation and these are used to show the response to increasing the number of features used in the splitting. Internal estimates are also used to measure variable importance. These ideas are also applicable to regression.

resources.title: Bias in random forest variable importance measures: Illustrations, sources and a solution
resources.abstract: BACKGROUND: Variable importance measures for random forests have been receiving increased attention as a means of variable selection in many classification tasks in bioinformatics and related scientific fields, for instance to select a subset of genetic markers relevant for the prediction of a certain disease. We show that random forest variable importance measures are a sensible means for variable selection in many applications, but are not reliable in situations where potential predictor variables vary in their scale of measurement or their number of categories. This is particularly important in genomics and computational biology, where predictors often include variables of different types, for example when predictors include both sequence data and continuous variables such as folding energy, or when amino acid sequence data show different numbers of categories. RESULTS: Simulation studies are presented illustrating that, when random forest variable importance measures are used with data of varying types, the results are misleading because suboptimal predictor variables may be artificially preferred in variable selection. The two mechanisms underlying this deficiency are biased variable selection in the individual classification trees used to build the random forest on one hand, and effects induced by bootstrap sampling with replacement on the other hand. CONCLUSION: We propose to employ an alternative implementation of random forests, that provides unbiased variable selection in the individual classification trees. When this method is applied using subsampling without replacement, the resulting variable importance measures can be used reliably for variable selection even in situations where the potential predictor variables vary in their scale of measurement or their number of categories. The usage of both random forest algorithms and their variable importance measures in the R system for statistical computing is illustrated and documented thoroughly in an application re-analyzing data from a study on RNA editing. Therefore the suggested method can be applied straightforwardly by scientists in bioinformatics research.

resources.title: A comparison of random forest and its Gini importance with standard chemometric methods for the feature selection and classification of spectral data
resources.abstract: Background Regularized regression methods such as principal component or partial least squares regression perform well in learning tasks on high dimensional spectral data, but cannot explicitly eliminate irrelevant features. The random forest classifier with its associated Gini feature importance, on the other hand, allows for an explicit feature elimination, but may not be optimally adapted to spectral data due to the topology of its constituent classification trees which are based on orthogonal splits in feature space. Results We propose to combine the best of both approaches, and evaluated the joint use of a feature selection based on a recursive feature elimination using the Gini importance of random forests' together with regularized classification methods on spectral data sets from medical diagnostics, chemotaxonomy, biomedical analytics, food science, and synthetically modified spectral data. Here, a feature selection using the Gini feature importance with a regularized classification by discriminant partial least squares regression performed as well as or better than a filtering according to different univariate statistical tests, or using regression coefficients in a backward feature elimination. It outperformed the direct application of the random forest classifier, or the direct application of the regularized classifiers on the full set of features. Conclusion The Gini importance of the random forest provided superior means for measuring feature relevance on spectral data, but – on an optimal subset of features – the regularized classifiers might be preferable over the random forest classifier, in spite of their limitation to model linear dependencies only. A feature selection based on Gini importance, however, may precede a regularized linear classification to identify this optimal subset of features, and to earn a double benefit of both dimensionality reduction and the elimination of noise from the classification task.

techniques.name: Coefficient Magnitudes (in Linear Models)
techniques.description: Coefficient Magnitudes explains a linear model by reading its fitted coefficients. Each coefficient shows how much the prediction changes when its feature rises by one unit while every other feature stays fixed, and its sign gives the direction. Because a coefficient's size depends on the units of its feature, the features are first put on a common scale, for example by standardising them or by multiplying each coefficient by its feature's standard deviation. The features with the largest scaled coefficients are then read as having the strongest influence on the model's predictions. This gives a global view of the model without needing a separate explanation method.

example_use_cases.description: An estate agency's data team standardises the inputs of a linear house-price model, then ranks the absolute coefficients to show valuers which property attributes move the estimate most. Valuers check that the signs match their experience, for example that more floor area raises the price, before the model guides asking prices.

A lender's model-risk team documents a linear credit-scoring model for its regulator by publishing the standardised coefficient of every input. The reviewer can read off the direction and relative weight of each input without a separate explanation tool, and can query any input that carries more weight than policy allows.

A public health analyst fits a logistic regression to predict emergency readmission and reports standardised coefficients to clinicians, who see which patient characteristics push the predicted risk up or down. The analyst refits on resamples first, to check that the large coefficients keep their sign.

limitations.description: Raw magnitudes have output-per-input units and cannot be ranked across differently scaled variables. Express comparable input changes explicitly; changing metres to centimetres makes the corresponding coefficient smaller for the same predictions.

Coefficients concern the encoded model inputs while other inputs are held fixed. If the model includes transformed variables or interactions, inspecting one coefficient does not give the whole effect of changing an original variable.

Correlated predictors can have unstable or shared coefficients even when predictions change little. Scaling does not remove this problem, and regularisation can change which correlated feature receives a large weight.

Each coefficient is conditional on the other features in the model. A feature can have a negative coefficient while rising with the outcome on its own, so a coefficient read in isolation can mislead about the feature's plain relationship to the outcome.

A coefficient is a conditional association in the fitted model, not a causal effect. Its magnitude alone also does not give a particular applicant's contribution, which depends on that applicant's feature values.

techniques.name: DeepLIFT
techniques.description: DeepLIFT (Deep Learning Important FeaTures) explains a single prediction of a neural network by dividing the difference between the model's output and its output on a reference input among the input features. The reference is a neutral input chosen for the problem, such as an all-zero image or a blurred copy of the input. The method measures how far each neuron's activation is from its value on the reference, then passes those differences backwards through the layers in one pass, applying a rule for each layer type. A plain gradient (the rate of change of the output with respect to an input) is zero where the output has levelled off, but DeepLIFT can still assign credit there. The scores add up to the output difference and mean something only relative to the reference chosen.

example_use_cases.description: A genomics group training a neural network to predict where a regulatory protein binds DNA computes DeepLIFT scores for each predicted binding region against a reference sequence with background base frequencies. They read off which short stretches of bases carry the score, compare them with known binding motifs, and decide whether the model has learned real regulatory sequence before using it to prioritise experiments.

A hospital imaging team is investigating a chest X-ray classifier that flags healthy patients as abnormal. For the false positives it computes DeepLIFT scores against a blurred copy of each image and checks whether the weight sits on the image border, where scanner labels are printed, rather than on lung tissue. It then decides whether to mask the labels and retrain.

A regional geohazard agency uses a neural network to rate landslide susceptibility from terrain, rainfall and land-cover layers. For a slope the model rates as high risk, DeepLIFT scores show which input layers drove the rating, and the agency compares them with the field investigation report before using the map for planning.

A lender's credit team sends each declined applicant a short statement of the factors that most lowered their score. For its neural network scorer it computes DeepLIFT scores against a documented reference applicant, the median approved applicant, and the statement lists the factors with the largest negative scores, which are the ones that pulled this score below the reference.

limitations.description: Every score is relative to a reference input, and the choice changes the picture. In the original paper an all-zero reference on CIFAR-10 images highlighted hard-to-interpret background pixels, while a blurred copy of the image highlighted object outlines. State the reference used and repeat the analysis with at least one alternative before drawing conclusions.

The Captum implementation supports only the Rescale rule, which can give all the credit to one of two inputs that jointly drive the output. In the paper's min(i1, i2) example Rescale scores only the smaller input, while the RevealCancel rule shares the credit. Where inputs interact, the scores can hide a dependency that a more complete rule would show.

Propagation rules must support the network operations. Captum implements the Rescale rule and a limited set of nonlinearities; inaccessible operations in built-in recurrent modules can prevent attribution unless a supported implementation is used.

Two networks that compute exactly the same function can receive different DeepLIFT scores, because differences between a neuron and its reference do not obey the chain rule that gradients obey (Sundararajan et al., 2017, App. B). The scores therefore describe how the model is built as well as what it computes, which matters when comparing a model with a re-implemented or compressed version of it.

Feature contributions account for a particular output difference, not a causal effect in the world or a guaranteed change after deleting that feature. Correlated genomic bases or financial variables make that distinction important.

resources.title: Learning Important Features Through Propagating Activation Differences
resources.abstract: The purported "black box" nature of neural networks is a barrier to adoption in applications where interpretability is essential. Here we present DeepLIFT (Deep Learning Important FeaTures), a method for decomposing the output prediction of a neural network on a specific input by backpropagating the contributions of all neurons in the network to every feature of the input. DeepLIFT compares the activation of each neuron to its 'reference activation' and assigns contribution scores according to the difference. By optionally giving separate consideration to positive and negative contributions, DeepLIFT can also reveal dependencies which are missed by other approaches. Scores can be computed efficiently in a single backward pass. We apply DeepLIFT to models trained on MNIST and simulated genomic data, and show significant advantages over gradient-based methods. Video tutorial: http://goo.gl/qKb7pL, ICML slides: bit.ly/deeplifticmlslides, ICML talk: https://vimeo.com/238275076, code: http://goo.gl/RM8jvH.

resources.title: An Attribution Deep Learning Interpretation Model for Landslide Susceptibility Mapping in the Three Gorges Reservoir Area
resources.abstract: Deep learning (DL) models are increasingly used for landslide susceptibility mapping (LSM) due to their higher accuracy. However, due to the lack of explanations of the influence of input contributing factors by current DL models, accurately identifying the cause of each landslide remains challenging. This study proposes a novel interpretable DL model named Deep-Attention-LSF, which assigns significance scores to contributing factors at local levels for attributing landslide susceptibility. This model considers the significance scores of input factors to more accurately predict landslide occurrence. DeepLIFT is used as an attribution branching network for interpreting the relationship between input factors and each landslide event. Subsequently, a landslide classification network formed by combining convolutional neural network and long short-term memory is used to predict the landslide occurrence in the entire study area. The performance of Deep-Attention-LSF is tested using the landslide inventory map of Three Gorges reservoir area and the associated maps of 18 landslide-related factors. The accuracy, recall, precision, and F1-score of our model were 0.9645, 0.9583, 0.9676, and 0.9522, respectively. These suggest that our model outperformed the compared models, including self-attention LSM, frequency-ratio-attention LSM, bagging and random subspace naive bayes tree, gradient boosting decision tree, random forest, information value model and enhanced C5.0 decision tree model. Deep-Attention-LSF provided reasonable explanations for landslide attributions by comparison with field investigation reports for four specific landslide cases. Combining the interpretation of Deep-Attention-LSF with field investigations can provide more comprehensive information for evaluating specific landslides, providing a useful tool for landslide prevention and management.

techniques.name: Layer-wise Relevance Propagation
techniques.description: Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) explains a neural network's prediction by working backwards from the output to the inputs. It treats the prediction score as a quantity called relevance, then passes that relevance back through each layer in proportion to how much each neuron contributed in the forward pass. The rules for this redistribution are chosen to keep the total relevance roughly constant from layer to layer, so the input scores add up to the prediction apart from small amounts absorbed by bias terms and stabilisers. Different rules can be used for different types of layer. The result is a relevance score for each input, such as a pixel or a feature, with positive values for inputs that supported the prediction and negative values for inputs that counted against it.

example_use_cases.description: Identifying which pixels in chest X-rays contribute to pneumonia detection, helping radiologists verify AI diagnoses by highlighting anatomical regions the model considers relevant.

A perception team investigating a misclassified traffic-sign image draws the relevance map for the wrong class. The map shows the relevance sitting on a sticker and the background rather than on the sign itself, which tells the team to add training images with such clutter before the model is retested.

A bank's model-risk reviewers receive LRP relevance scores for a sample of declined applications scored by a neural network. They check that the inputs with the most relevance for the decline output are affordability measures and not proxy fields such as postcode, and file the scores with the decision record for audit.

limitations.description: Each layer type needs its own propagation rule, and a new layer type has none until someone derives one, so adapting LRP to a new architecture takes expertise and testing.
Rule selection (LRP-ε, LRP-γ and others) changes the resulting maps, so two analysts can produce different explanations of the same prediction, and choosing among them takes expertise.

Heatmaps are hard to validate. The original paper judges them by eye and with a pixel-flipping test, and notes that quality beyond visual assessment is an open question, so a plausible-looking map does not prove the model relies on the highlighted inputs.

Standard rules do not cover attention layers. Extensions for transformers, such as AttnLRP in the LXT library, exist but are recent and specific to certain architectures, so users of transformers or large language models must adopt them and confirm they match their model.

Bias handling and epsilon stabilisation can absorb or inject relevance, so input scores do not always sum exactly to the selected output. A report should document the accounting residual before claiming conservation.

resources.title: On Pixel-Wise Explanations for Non-Linear Classifier Decisions by Layer-Wise Relevance Propagation
resources.abstract: Understanding and interpreting classification decisions of automated image classification systems is of high value in many applications, as it allows to verify the reasoning of the system and provides additional information to the human expert. Although machine learning methods are solving very successfully a plethora of tasks, they have in most cases the disadvantage of acting as a black box, not providing any information about what made them arrive at a particular decision. This work proposes a general solution to the problem of understanding classification decisions by pixel-wise decomposition of nonlinear classifiers. We introduce a methodology that allows to visualize the contributions of single pixels to predictions for kernel-based classifiers over Bag of Words features and for multilayered neural networks. These pixel contributions can be visualized as heatmaps and are provided to a human expert who can intuitively not only verify the validity of the classification decision, but also focus further analysis on regions of potential interest. We evaluate our method for classifiers trained on PASCAL VOC 2009 images, synthetic image data containing geometric shapes, the MNIST handwritten digits data set and for the pre-trained ImageNet model available as part of the Caffe open source package.

resources.title: Layer-Wise Relevance Propagation: An Overview
Layer-Wise Relevance Propagation for Explaining Deep Neural Network Decisions in MRI-Based Alzheimer's Disease Classification
resources.abstract: Deep neural networks have led to state-of-the-art results in many medical imaging tasks including Alzheimer's disease (AD) detection based on structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data. However, the network decisions are often perceived as being highly non-transparent, making it difficult to apply these algorithms in clinical routine. In this study, we propose using layer-wise relevance propagation (LRP) to visualize convolutional neural network decisions for AD based on MRI data. Similarly to other visualization methods, LRP produces a heatmap in the input space indicating the importance/relevance of each voxel contributing to the final classification outcome. In contrast to susceptibility maps produced by guided backpropagation ("Which change in voxels would change the outcome most?"), the LRP method is able to directly highlight positive contributions to the network classification in the input space. In particular, we show that (1) the LRP method is very specific for individuals ("Why does this person have AD?") with high inter-patient variability, (2) there is very little relevance for AD in healthy controls and (3) areas that exhibit a lot of relevance correlate well with what is known from literature. To quantify the latter, we compute size-corrected metrics of the summed relevance per brain area, e.g., relevance density or relevance gain. Although these metrics produce very individual "fingerprints" of relevance patterns for AD patients, a lot of importance is put on areas in the temporal lobe including the hippocampus. After discussing several limitations such as sensitivity toward the underlying model and computation parameters, we conclude that LRP might have a high potential to assist clinicians in explaining neural network decisions for diagnosing AD (and potentially other diseases) based on structural MRI data.

techniques.name: Contextual Decomposition
techniques.description: Contextual Decomposition explains why an LSTM, a neural network that reads text one word at a time, made a particular prediction. The user picks a word or phrase, and the method splits the network's output score into two parts: the part due to that phrase alone, and the part due to everything else, including how the phrase interacts with the words around it. Comparing a phrase's score with the scores of its parts reveals effects that word-by-word methods miss, such as a negation reversing the sentiment of the word that follows it. The split is tracked through the LSTM's internal gates, so the model itself is not changed or retrained. The output is a numerical score for each phrase examined.

example_use_cases.description: Analysing why an LSTM-based spam filter flagged an email by decomposing contributions from individual words ('free', 'urgent') versus their contextual interactions ('free trial' together).

A hospital analytics team checks an LSTM that flags clinical notes mentioning possible pneumonia. Contextual decomposition shows whether negated findings such as 'no evidence of pneumonia' push the score down, as intended, or whether the model reacts to the word 'pneumonia' alone, which tells the team if it needs retraining on negated examples before use.

A platform's trust-and-safety team handles an appeal against an LSTM toxicity classifier's removal of a post. The reviewing moderator is shown the phrases with the highest contextual decomposition scores, including whether a negation such as 'not stupid' was read correctly, so the moderator can judge whether the removal rested on the post's actual meaning.

limitations.description: Developed for LSTMs, whose gates the method uses to separate a phrase's own effect from its interactions. The source does not cover plain recurrent networks, transformers or attention models, so teams using those cannot apply the published method as it stands.
Needs internal states, gate parameters and classifier weights. Output labels or probabilities alone do not reveal the phrase-related and remaining-input components.

The user must choose each phrase to examine, and the published method handles contiguous phrases. The number of possible phrases grows quickly with text length, so scanning a whole document for interactions is costly and easy to leave incomplete.

The split relies on linearising the gate and activation functions and averaging over orderings of the terms. Interaction scores are therefore approximate, and the source validates them only on sentiment tasks (Stanford Sentiment Treebank, Yelp), so scores on other tasks need checking independently.

Components combine additively in hidden states and class scores before the probability transformation. They should not be read as independent probabilities or as the exact effect of deleting a phrase.

resources.title: Beyond Word Importance: Contextual Decomposition to Extract Interactions from LSTMs
resources.abstract: The driving force behind the recent success of LSTMs has been their ability to learn complex and non-linear relationships. Consequently, our inability to describe these relationships has led to LSTMs being characterized as black boxes. To this end, we introduce contextual decomposition (CD), an interpretation algorithm for analysing individual predictions made by standard LSTMs, without any changes to the underlying model. By decomposing the output of a LSTM, CD captures the contributions of combinations of words or variables to the final prediction of an LSTM. On the task of sentiment analysis with the Yelp and SST data sets, we show that CD is able to reliably identify words and phrases of contrasting sentiment, and how they are combined to yield the LSTM's final prediction. Using the phrase-level labels in SST, we also demonstrate that CD is able to successfully extract positive and negative negations from an LSTM, something which has not previously been done.

resources.title: Interpreting patient-Specific risk prediction using contextual decomposition of BiLSTMs: Application to children with asthma
resources.abstract: Background Predictive modeling with longitudinal electronic health record (EHR) data offers great promise for accelerating personalized medicine and better informs clinical decision-making. Recently, deep learning models have achieved state-of-the-art performance for many healthcare prediction tasks. However, deep models lack interpretability, which is integral to successful decision-making and can lead to better patient care. In this paper, we build upon the contextual decomposition (CD) method, an algorithm for producing importance scores from long short-term memory networks (LSTMs). We extend the method to bidirectional LSTMs (BiLSTMs) and use it in the context of predicting future clinical outcomes using patients’ EHR historical visits. Methods We use a real EHR dataset comprising 11071 patients, to evaluate and compare CD interpretations from LSTM and BiLSTM models. First, we train LSTM and BiLSTM models for the task of predicting which pre-school children with respiratory system-related complications will have asthma at school-age. After that, we conduct quantitative and qualitative analysis to evaluate the CD interpretations produced by the contextual decomposition of the trained models. In addition, we develop an interactive visualization to demonstrate the utility of CD scores in explaining predicted outcomes. Results Our experimental evaluation demonstrate that whenever a clear visit-level pattern exists, the models learn that pattern and the contextual decomposition can appropriately attribute the prediction to the correct pattern. In addition, the results confirm that the CD scores agree to a large extent with the importance scores generated using logistic regression coefficients. Our main insight was that rather than interpreting the attribution of individual visits to the predicted outcome, we could instead attribute a model’s prediction to a group of visits. Conclusion We presented a quantitative and qualitative evidence that CD interpretations can explain patient-specific predictions using CD attributions of individual visits or a group of visits.

techniques.name: Taylor Decomposition
techniques.description: Taylor Decomposition explains one prediction of a neural network by splitting its output score into a contribution from each input, such as each pixel. It starts from a reference input, called a root point, that is close to the real input but for which the network's score is zero. Each input's contribution is the slope of the score with respect to that input at the root point, multiplied by how far the input sits from the root, and terms that involve several inputs at once are left out. Finding a good root point is slow for large networks, so the deep variant applies the same idea to one neuron at a time and passes the contributions backwards through the layers, which gives rules close to those of Layer-wise Relevance Propagation. The result is a relevance score for every input that can be drawn as a heatmap.

example_use_cases.description: A quality team uses a convolutional network to flag defective printed circuit boards. For each flagged board they draw the deep Taylor heatmap and check that the highlighted pixels sit on the defect and not on a board label, the edge or the background, before they trust the flags enough to stop manual inspection.

A hospital's model-validation group audits a ReLU network that classifies chest X-rays. For a sample of positive cases, deep Taylor relevance shows whether the evidence for the finding lies inside the lungs or on markers, text or borders added by the imaging equipment, before the group signs the model off for a pilot.

A bank's data science team has a ReLU network that scores small-business loan applications from tabular inputs. For a declined application, deep Taylor relevance lists which inputs supplied most of the score, so a reviewer can see whether the decision rests on repayment history and income or on a field such as postcode.

limitations.description: The explanation depends on the choice of root point, and different reference inputs give different attributions. Finding the nearest root needs an iterative optimisation that is slow for large networks and may not converge, which is why the source applies the deep variant to large image networks.

Plain Taylor decomposition uses only first-order terms, so joint effects of several inputs stay unattributed and the scores need not add up to the prediction. In the source's tests the nearest-root version lost a large share of the relevance, so its heatmaps can leave much of the prediction unexplained.

The deep variant's guarantees, scores that add up to the prediction and are never negative, are proved for ReLU-style layers with zero or negative biases, and iNNvestigate documents support for ReLU networks only. Other activations, positive biases or normalisation layers need workarounds that the proofs do not cover.

Heatmaps explain one input at a time and are hard to validate. The source judges them by eye and by checking that relevance is conserved on MNIST digits and ImageNet photos, so a plausible-looking map does not prove that the model relies on the highlighted inputs.

Requires access to internal layer operations and supported redistribution rules. A prediction-only service cannot supply this layer-wise decomposition, and an image-derived rule should not be assumed valid for arbitrary text or attention models.

resources.title: Explaining NonLinear Classification Decisions with Deep Taylor Decomposition
resources.abstract: Nonlinear methods such as Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) are the gold standard for various challenging machine learning problems, e.g., image classification, natural language processing or human action recognition. Although these methods perform impressively well, they have a significant disadvantage, the lack of transparency, limiting the interpretability of the solution and thus the scope of application in practice. Especially DNNs act as black boxes due to their multilayer nonlinear structure. In this paper we introduce a novel methodology for interpreting generic multilayer neural networks by decomposing the network classification decision into contributions of its input elements. Although our focus is on image classification, the method is applicable to a broad set of input data, learning tasks and network architectures. Our method is based on deep Taylor decomposition and efficiently utilizes the structure of the network by backpropagating the explanations from the output to the input layer. We evaluate the proposed method empirically on the MNIST and ILSVRC data sets.

techniques.name: Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping
techniques.description: Grad-CAM (Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping) draws a heatmap over an image showing which regions most raise a convolutional neural network's score for a chosen class, which need not be the one the model predicted. The last convolutional layer produces a stack of feature maps, each a coarse grid recording where one learned pattern appears. Grad-CAM takes the gradient of the class score with respect to each map (how much the score changes as that map's values change), averages it to give the map a weight, and adds the weighted maps together. It keeps only the positive values, so the result marks regions that count in favour of the class, then enlarges the coarse grid to the image's size and lays it over the image, so the output shows broad regions rather than pixels. In a bias-diagnosis use, the maps are laid over the errors of a classifier already known to err more for one group, to see which image region the model relies on; the group-wise errors and the training-data counts come from separate checks.

example_use_cases.description: A dermatology AI team validating a melanoma classifier overlays Grad-CAM on dermoscopy images and compares the highlighted region with the lesion outline drawn by a clinician. Cases where the heat falls on a ruler, hair or skin markings are collected, and the team decides whether the training images need cleaning before the model goes to clinical evaluation.

A team developing the traffic sign recogniser for a driver assistance system overlays Grad-CAM on the test images it misclassifies. When the heat sits on the background or a shadow rather than on the sign, they add training images with similar backgrounds and lighting, then recheck the overlays before the release decision.

A team studying dataset bias fine-tunes an image classifier to separate doctors from nurses in photographs and finds, on a gender-balanced test set, that it errs far more often for one gender. It overlays Grad-CAM on those errors: heat on faces and hairstyles rather than on uniforms or equipment shows the model has learned a gender shortcut, and a count of the training photographs by gender shows why. The team rebalances the photographs, retrains and checks that the heat moves.

limitations.description: Needs the network's gradients and its last convolutional feature maps, so it cannot be run on a model reached only through an API, or on architectures without convolutional layers. The user must also choose which layer to use, and the paper reports that maps become progressively worse for earlier layers (Selvaraju et al., Sec 3).

The map has the resolution of the last convolutional layer (14 by 14 for VGG-16 and AlexNet), then is enlarged to the image. Small or irregular findings, such as a few-millimetre lesion or a thin sign pole, fall inside one or two cells, so the overlay cannot show whether the model attended to the finding or to its surroundings.

In a chest X-ray benchmark Grad-CAM generally located pathologies better than six other saliency methods but worse than radiologists, with the largest gap for small, complex-shaped findings, and it located them better when the model was confident (Saporta et al., 2022). The overlays are least reliable for the uncertain, hard cases where a reviewer most wants an explanation.

A bright region means features there raise the class score under a local linear approximation, not that the model relied on them. In the paper's own check, Grad-CAM's ranking of image patches agreed only moderately with occlusion, which masks patches and re-scores the image (rank correlation 0.254, Sec 5.3). The ReLU also hides regions that count against the class.

resources.title: Grad-CAM: Visual Explanations from Deep Networks via Gradient-based Localization
resources.abstract: We propose a technique for producing "visual explanations" for decisions from a large class of CNN-based models, making them more transparent. Our approach - Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM), uses the gradients of any target concept, flowing into the final convolutional layer to produce a coarse localization map highlighting important regions in the image for predicting the concept. Grad-CAM is applicable to a wide variety of CNN model-families: (1) CNNs with fully-connected layers, (2) CNNs used for structured outputs, (3) CNNs used in tasks with multimodal inputs or reinforcement learning, without any architectural changes or re-training. We combine Grad-CAM with fine-grained visualizations to create a high-resolution class-discriminative visualization and apply it to off-the-shelf image classification, captioning, and visual question answering (VQA) models, including ResNet-based architectures. In the context of image classification models, our visualizations (a) lend insights into their failure modes, (b) are robust to adversarial images, (c) outperform previous methods on localization, (d) are more faithful to the underlying model and (e) help achieve generalization by identifying dataset bias. For captioning and VQA, we show that even non-attention based models can localize inputs. We devise a way to identify important neurons through Grad-CAM and combine it with neuron names to provide textual explanations for model decisions. Finally, we design and conduct human studies to measure if Grad-CAM helps users establish appropriate trust in predictions from models and show that Grad-CAM helps untrained users successfully discern a 'stronger' nodel from a 'weaker' one even when both make identical predictions. Our code is available at https://github.com/ramprs/grad-cam/, along with a demo at http://gradcam.cloudcv.org, and a video at youtu.be/COjUB9Izk6E.

resources.title: A Tutorial on Explainable Image Classification for Dementia Stages Using Convolutional Neural Network and Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping
resources.abstract: This paper presents a tutorial of an explainable approach using Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) and Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) to classify four progressive dementia stages based on open MRI brain images. The detailed implementation steps are demonstrated with an explanation. Whilst the proposed CNN architecture is demonstrated to achieve more than 99% accuracy for the test dataset, the computational procedure of CNN remains a black box. The visualisation based on Grad-CAM is attempted to explain such very high accuracy and may provide useful information for physicians. Future motivation based on this work is discussed.

resources.title: Benchmarking saliency methods for chest X-ray interpretation
resources.abstract: Saliency methods, which produce heat maps that highlight the areas of the medical image that influence model prediction, are often presented to clinicians as an aid in diagnostic decision-making. However, rigorous investigation of the accuracy and reliability of these strategies is necessary before they are integrated into the clinical setting. In this work, we quantitatively evaluate seven saliency methods, including Grad-CAM, across multiple neural network architectures using two evaluation metrics. We establish the first human benchmark for chest X-ray segmentation in a multilabel classification set-up, and examine under what clinical conditions saliency maps might be more prone to failure in localizing important pathologies compared with a human expert benchmark. We find that (1) while Grad-CAM generally localized pathologies better than the other evaluated saliency methods, all seven performed significantly worse compared with the human benchmark, (2) the gap in localization performance between Grad-CAM and the human benchmark was largest for pathologies that were smaller in size and had shapes that were more complex, and (3) model confidence was positively correlated with Grad-CAM localization performance. Our work demonstrates that several important limitations of saliency methods must be addressed before we can rely on them for deep learning explainability in medical imaging.

techniques.name: Influence Functions
techniques.description: Influence functions estimate which training examples most affected a model's prediction on a particular test example. For each training example, they estimate how much the model's loss on the test example would change if that example counted slightly more or slightly less, which approximates removing it and retraining without actually doing so. The estimate combines the gradient of the loss at the test and training points with the Hessian (the matrix of second derivatives, which describes the curvature of the training loss). The output ranks training examples as helpful or harmful for that prediction; because the theory assumes a smooth, convex loss, for deep networks the ranking is approximate, pointing to examples worth inspecting for mislabelled or unrepresentative cases rather than proving why the model erred. In a bias-diagnosis use, the rejections of a group already known from a separate check to be rejected more often are explained one by one, to find the training records that drive them.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital analytics team finds that its readmission model misclassifies many children. For a misclassified child, influence functions single out a handful of paediatric training records with far more influence than any others, showing that the training data holds very few children. The team collects more paediatric data before deciding whether the model can be used on that group.

An email-security team asks why its spam filter blocked a legitimate supplier invoice. It lists the training emails with the most influence on that decision, finds near-duplicate phishing messages with a similar layout, and decides whether to relabel, remove or down-weight them before retraining the filter.

A bank's model-risk team has found, from a separate check of approval rates by group, that applicants from one protected group are rejected more often. It takes a sample of that group's rejected applications and lists, for each, the training loans with the greatest influence on the rejection. It reviews whether those records are historical rejections made under discontinued underwriting rules or by branches with a known bias, and decides whether to remove or re-weight them.

limitations.description: Exact influence needs the inverse of the Hessian, which is out of reach for networks with millions of parameters. Implementations approximate it with Hessian-vector products or block-diagonal and low-rank forms, which still costs extra passes over the training data for every prediction explained and adds error. Plan to explain a sample of decisions, not all of them.

Needs the full training set, the loss function and parameters at or near a minimum of the training loss. A model delivered as an API or a finished file, or trained on data the assessor cannot see, cannot be examined. For models that are early-stopped or not trained to a minimum, the paper adds a damping term to the Hessian, one more setting that can change the ranking.

The derivation assumes a convex, twice-differentiable loss. On a non-convex CNN the paper still found a 0.86 correlation with actual retraining, but a larger study found estimates often erroneous for deeper networks and dependent on architecture, weight decay and the test point (Basu et al., 2020). Check the estimates against real retraining on a few examples before relying on them.

Losses with kinks, such as the hinge loss of a support vector machine, break the method. In the paper, influence computed on the unsmoothed hinge loss considerably overestimated the effect of removal, and a smooth approximation of the loss was needed. Check that the loss is smooth for the model in hand, or smooth it for the calculation.

resources.title: Understanding Black-box Predictions via Influence Functions
resources.abstract: How can we explain the predictions of a black-box model? In this paper, we use influence functions — a classic technique from robust statistics — to trace a model's prediction through the learning algorithm and back to its training data, thereby identifying training points most responsible for a given prediction. To scale up influence functions to modern machine learning settings, we develop a simple, efficient implementation that requires only oracle access to gradients and Hessian-vector products. We show that even on non-convex and non-differentiable models where the theory breaks down, approximations to influence functions can still provide valuable information. On linear models and convolutional neural networks, we demonstrate that influence functions are useful for multiple purposes: understanding model behavior, debugging models, detecting dataset errors, and even creating visually-indistinguishable training-set attacks.

resources.abstract: Modern deep learning models for NLP are notoriously opaque.This has motivated the development of methods for interpreting such models, e.g., via gradient-based saliency maps or the visualization of attention weights.Such approaches aim to provide explanations for a particular model prediction by highlighting important words in the corresponding input text.While this might be useful for tasks where decisions are explicitly influenced by individual tokens in the input, we suspect that such highlighting is not always suitable for tasks where model decisions should be driven by more complex reasoning.In this work, we investigate the use of influence functions for NLP, providing an alternative approach to interpreting neural text classifiers.Influence functions explain the decisions of a model by identifying influential training examples.Despite the promise of this approach, influence functions have not yet been extensively evaluated in the context of NLP, a gap addressed by this work.We conduct a comparison between influence functions and common word-saliency methods on representative tasks.As suspected, we find that influence functions are particularly useful for natural language inference, a task in which 'saliency maps' may not provide clear interpretation.Furthermore, we develop a new quantitative measure based on influence functions that can reveal artifacts in training data.

techniques.name: Contrastive Explanation Method
techniques.description: The Contrastive Explanation Method (CEM) explains one prediction of a classifier, such as a neural network, by describing what is present and what is absent in the input. A pertinent positive is the smallest set of features already present that is enough for the model to give the same prediction. A pertinent negative is the smallest set of features not currently present that would change the prediction to a different class if they were added. CEM finds both by solving an optimisation problem that searches for the smallest change to the input, and it can use an autoencoder (a model trained to reconstruct realistic inputs) to keep the changed inputs realistic. An explanation reads like 'this digit is a 3 because these strokes are present and because a short bar at the top is absent', since adding that bar would make it a 5.

example_use_cases.description: A procurement team uses a neural-network model that rates invoices as low, medium or high risk. For a high-risk invoice, the pertinent positives are the few triggered events that are enough for that rating, such as a large amount and a vendor with only a PO box. The pertinent negatives are events that did not occur but would lower the rating if they had, such as the vendor being registered. Reviewers check both before blocking payment.

A clinician reviews a decision-support model that suggests flu rather than pneumonia for a patient. The pertinent positives are the findings that are enough for that suggestion, such as cough, cold and fever. The pertinent negatives are findings that are absent but would move the suggestion to pneumonia if present, such as sputum and chills. The clinician compares both with their own reasoning to judge whether the model weighs the right findings.

A council uses a model to screen applications for housing support. When an application is declined, the pertinent negatives show which missing items, such as proof of tenancy, would have changed the outcome if present. A caseworker checks that each item is something the applicant can provide, then includes it in the decision notice.

limitations.description: Each explanation needs its own optimisation run for a single instance, so explaining many decisions is slow. Models whose gradients cannot be accessed need numerical gradient estimates, which slows it further.

Several settings shape the result, including how strongly the search favours small changes, how confident the model must be in the new class, and whether an autoencoder is used. Different settings can give different pertinent positives and negatives for the same instance, so they need checking with someone who knows the domain.

Changed inputs can be unrealistic. Without an autoencoder trained on good-quality data, a pertinent negative may describe an input that could never occur, so the explanation says little about real cases. Where data is scarce or poor, a good autoencoder may not be possible.

Absence has to be defined by the user. CEM adds or removes features relative to a value that stands for no signal, such as a blank pixel, and a poor choice gives meaningless pertinent negatives. This is natural for images and binary indicators, and needs domain judgement for continuous or categorical tabular data.

A pertinent negative is the smallest change the model responds to, not advice a person can act on. It may involve a feature that cannot be changed, such as age, and nothing in the method checks that the change is feasible. It is most useful when the two classes are close; if they are very different, there can be too many pertinent negatives to read.

resources.title: Explanations based on the Missing: Towards Contrastive Explanations with Pertinent Negatives
resources.abstract: In this paper we propose a novel method that provides contrastive explanations justifying the classification of an input by a black box classifier such as a deep neural network. Given an input we find what should be %necessarily and minimally and sufficiently present (viz. important object pixels in an image) to justify its classification and analogously what should be minimally and necessarily \emph{absent} (viz. certain background pixels). We argue that such explanations are natural for humans and are used commonly in domains such as health care and criminology. What is minimally but critically \emph{absent} is an important part of an explanation, which to the best of our knowledge, has not been explicitly identified by current explanation methods that explain predictions of neural networks. We validate our approach on three real datasets obtained from diverse domains; namely, a handwritten digits dataset MNIST, a large procurement fraud dataset and a brain activity strength dataset. In all three cases, we witness the power of our approach in generating precise explanations that are also easy for human experts to understand and evaluate.

Understanding How CNNs Recognize Facial Expressions: A Case Study with LIME and CEM
resources.abstract: Recognizing facial expressions has been a persistent goal in the scientific community. Since the rise of artificial intelligence, convolutional neural networks (CNN) have become popular to recognize facial expressions, as images can be directly used as input. Current CNN models can achieve high recognition rates, but they give no clue about their reasoning process. Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) has been developed as a means to help to interpret the results obtained by machine learning models. When dealing with images, one of the most-used XAI techniques is LIME. LIME highlights the areas of the image that contribute to a classification. As an alternative to LIME, the CEM method appeared, providing explanations in a way that is natural for human classification: besides highlighting what is sufficient to justify a classification, it also identifies what should be absent to maintain it and to distinguish it from another classification. This study presents the results of comparing LIME and CEM applied over complex images such as facial expression images. While CEM could be used to explain the results on images described with a reduced number of features, LIME would be the method of choice when dealing with images described with a huge number of features.

techniques.name: Out-of-Distribution Detector for Neural Networks
techniques.description: ODIN (Out-of-Distribution Detector for Neural Networks) flags inputs that look unlike the data a neural network classifier was trained on, and it works on an already trained network without retraining it. A classifier reports a confidence score, the highest probability it gives to any class, but that score is often high even for unfamiliar inputs. ODIN adjusts the score in two ways so that familiar and unfamiliar inputs separate better. It divides the classifier's raw output scores by a large constant, called the temperature, before turning them into probabilities, and it nudges the input slightly in the direction that raises the score, which lifts familiar inputs more than unfamiliar ones. An input whose adjusted score falls below a chosen threshold is flagged as out-of-distribution, so its prediction can be withheld or referred for review.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital screens each chest X-ray with ODIN before the diagnostic classifier's result is shown. Scans that are not chest X-rays, or that carry heavy artefacts, are flagged for human review instead of receiving a confident diagnosis, and the false positive rate is measured on a sample of such scans first.

An automated driving team scores each camera frame with ODIN and passes frames below the threshold to a fallback routine, such as slowing the vehicle and requesting remote assistance. The team measures how many unfamiliar frames, such as sensor faults or unusual scenes, are wrongly accepted before relying on the detector.

limitations.description: Temperature and perturbation size are tuned on a validation set that includes out-of-distribution examples, so some representative unfamiliar data is needed before deployment. The paper found settings transferred reasonably between validation sets, but only on image benchmarks.

Detection gets harder as unfamiliar inputs resemble the training data. In the original paper, at 95% acceptance of familiar images, the share of unfamiliar natural images wrongly accepted rose from at most about 11% with a 10-class training set to between 19% and 58% with a 100-class one, so performance must be measured on the deployment's own data.
Not designed to resist inputs deliberately crafted to look in-distribution, and the original paper does not evaluate adversarial evasion, so it gives no protection against a deliberate attacker.
Needs access to the network's gradients to compute the input perturbation, so it cannot be applied to a model that is reachable only through an API.
Each input needs at least one extra forward pass and one backward pass before the final scoring pass, which can matter for real-time or high-volume use.

resources.title: Enhancing The Reliability of Out-of-distribution Image Detection in Neural Networks
resources.abstract: We consider the problem of detecting out-of-distribution images in neural networks. We propose ODIN, a simple and effective method that does not require any change to a pre-trained neural network. Our method is based on the observation that using temperature scaling and adding small perturbations to the input can separate the softmax score distributions between in- and out-of-distribution images, allowing for more effective detection. We show in a series of experiments that ODIN is compatible with diverse network architectures and datasets. It consistently outperforms the baseline approach by a large margin, establishing a new state-of-the-art performance on this task. For example, ODIN reduces the false positive rate from the baseline 34.7% to 4.3% on the DenseNet (applied to CIFAR-10) when the true positive rate is 95%.

resources.title: Confidence-Based Out-of-Distribution Detection: A Comparative Study and Analysis
resources.abstract: Image classification models deployed in the real world may receive inputs outside the intended data distribution. For critical applications such as clinical decision making, it is important that a model can detect such out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs and express its uncertainty. In this work, we assess the capability of various state-of-the-art approaches for confidence-based OOD detection through a comparative study and in-depth analysis. First, we leverage a computer vision benchmark to reproduce and compare multiple OOD detection methods. We then evaluate their capabilities on the challenging task of disease classification using chest X-rays. Our study shows that high performance in a computer vision task does not directly translate to accuracy in a medical imaging task. We analyse factors that affect performance of the methods between the two tasks. Our results provide useful insights for developing the next generation of OOD detection methods.

techniques.name: Adversarial Debiasing
techniques.description: Adversarial debiasing trains a model so that its predictions carry as little information as possible about a protected attribute, such as sex or race. Two neural networks are trained together, a predictor that learns the main task, such as estimating default risk, and an adversary that tries to guess each person's protected attribute from the predictor's output. The predictor is updated to stay accurate while making the adversary's guesses fail, which pushes its outputs towards equal rates of favourable outcomes across groups (demographic parity). If the adversary is also given the true label, the predictor is penalised only for information about the attribute beyond what the label carries, which targets equal error rates across groups (equalised odds). The method needs the protected attribute for every training example and a model trained by gradient descent.

example_use_cases.description: A technology company trains a CV-screening model with an adversary that tries to guess each applicant's gender from the model's shortlisting score, so that selection rates come out similar for men and women (demographic parity) instead of leaning on CV features that happen to correlate with gender.

A lender trains a default-risk model for loan approvals with an adversary that is given each applicant's score and true repayment outcome and tries to guess their age band, so that false-positive and false-negative rates are similar across age bands (equalised odds) while predictive accuracy is kept.

A hospital group trains a COVID-19 screening model on emergency-department data with an adversary that tries to guess patient ethnicity from the model's score and the true test result, so that error rates are similar across ethnic groups while screening performance stays clinically useful.

limitations.description: The adversary only sees what it is given, usually the predictor's score and, for equalised odds, the true label. The method therefore targets one output-level criterion and gives no assurance that hidden layers are free of protected-attribute information, or that a different criterion holds.
Needs the protected attribute for every training example, so it cannot be used where that attribute was never collected or may not be held.

Demographic parity and equalised odds generally cannot both be met, so one must be chosen before training. Equal error rates can also come from worsening one group's rates: in the original Adult income experiment, the false-positive rate for women rose from 0.025 to 0.065.

Training two networks against each other is unstable. The weight given to the adversary has to be tuned (adversary_loss_weight in AIF360), and a wrong setting can make training diverge or leave the result closer to a different criterion than the one intended.

The paper's guarantee that outputs meet the chosen criterion holds only if both networks converge and the adversary is strong enough. A weak adversary leaves bias in place, and the convexity assumptions behind the proof do not hold for typical neural networks, so fairness has to be checked on held-out data after training.

resources.title: On the Fairness ROAD: Robust Optimization for Adversarial Debiasing
resources.abstract: In the field of algorithmic fairness, significant attention has been put on group fairness criteria, such as Demographic Parity and Equalized Odds. Nevertheless, these objectives, measured as global averages, have raised concerns about persistent local disparities between sensitive groups. In this work, we address the problem of local fairness, which ensures that the predictor is unbiased not only in terms of expectations over the whole population, but also within any subregion of the feature space, unknown at training time. To enforce this objective, we introduce ROAD, a novel approach that leverages the Distributionally Robust Optimization (DRO) framework within a fair adversarial learning objective, where an adversary tries to infer the sensitive attribute from the predictions. Using an instance-level re-weighting strategy, ROAD is designed to prioritize inputs that are likely to be locally unfair, i.e. where the adversary faces the least difficulty in reconstructing the sensitive attribute. Numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our method: it achieves Pareto dominance with respect to local fairness and accuracy for a given global fairness level across three standard datasets, and also enhances fairness generalization under distribution shift.

resources.title: Mitigating Unwanted Biases with Adversarial Learning
resources.abstract: Machine learning is a tool for building models that accurately represent input training data. When undesired biases concerning demographic groups are in the training data, well-trained models will reflect those biases. We present a framework for mitigating such biases by including a variable for the group of interest and simultaneously learning a predictor and an adversary. The input to the network X, here text or census data, produces a prediction Y, such as an analogy completion or income bracket, while the adversary tries to model a protected variable Z, here gender or zip code. The objective is to maximize the predictor's ability to predict Y while minimizing the adversary's ability to predict Z. Applied to analogy completion, this method results in accurate predictions that exhibit less evidence of stereotyping Z. When applied to a classification task using the UCI Adult (Census) Dataset, it results in a predictive model that does not lose much accuracy while achieving very close to equality of odds (Hardt, et al., 2016). The method is flexible and applicable to multiple definitions of fairness as well as a wide range of gradient-based learning models, including both regression and classification tasks.

resources.title: An adversarial training framework for mitigating algorithmic biases in clinical machine learning
resources.abstract: Machine learning is becoming increasingly prominent in healthcare. Although its benefits are clear, growing attention is being given to how these tools may exacerbate existing biases and disparities. In this study, we introduce an adversarial training framework that is capable of mitigating biases that may have been acquired through data collection. We demonstrate this proposed framework on the real-world task of rapidly predicting COVID-19, and focus on mitigating site-specific (hospital) and demographic (ethnicity) biases. Using the statistical definition of equalized odds, we show that adversarial training improves outcome fairness, while still achieving clinically-effective screening performances (negative predictive values >0.98). We compare our method to previous benchmarks, and perform prospective and external validation across four independent hospital cohorts. Our method can be generalized to any outcomes, models, and definitions of fairness.

sample_claims.text: On held-out data, the shortlisting model's selection rates differ between gender groups by no more than the agreed tolerance, and its accuracy is within the agreed margin of the unconstrained model.
The default-risk model's false-positive and false-negative rates differ between age bands by no more than the agreed tolerance on held-out data.
The COVID-19 screening model's error rates are similar across ethnic groups in each external hospital cohort, with negative predictive value above the clinical threshold set for screening.
Compared with the same model trained without the adversary, the model's gap on the chosen fairness criterion is smaller on held-out data, at a reported cost in accuracy.

techniques.name: Federated Learning
techniques.description: Federated learning trains one shared model across several parties, such as phones or hospitals, without collecting their data in one place. Each party trains the current model on its own data and sends back only an update, such as the changed weights (the model's internal numbers) or the gradients (the direction of change). A central coordinator combines the updates, typically by averaging, into an improved shared model and sends it out again, and the cycle repeats over many rounds. Raw records stay with their owners, which limits how much sensitive data is stored or moved and can support data protection rules that favour collecting less. It is not a privacy guarantee on its own, because updates can still reveal information about the data behind them and the coordinator has to be trusted.

example_use_cases.description: A mobile keyboard team trains a next-word prediction model on users' phones and receives only model updates, so typed text never reaches its servers. The team uses this to decide whether personalised suggestions can ship without collecting message content centrally.

Hospitals in several countries train a model that predicts COVID-19 outcomes on their own patient records and share only model updates with a coordinating centre, so no patient record leaves a hospital. Each hospital's data governance board uses this to decide whether it can join the collaboration.

Several banks jointly train a fraud-detection model on their own transaction data and share only model updates, so no bank's customer records reach a competitor. Each bank's compliance team uses the setup to decide whether joint training fits its data-sharing restrictions.

limitations.description: Communication overhead can be substantial, especially with frequent model updates and large models, potentially limiting scalability and increasing training time compared to centralised approaches.

Statistical heterogeneity across participants (non-IID data distributions) can lead to training instability, slower convergence, and reduced model performance compared to centralised training on pooled data.
System heterogeneity in computational capabilities, network connectivity, and availability of participating devices can create bottlenecks and introduce bias towards more capable participants.
Privacy vulnerabilities remain through gradient leakage attacks, model inversion, and membership inference attacks that can potentially reconstruct sensitive information from shared model updates.

A faulty or malicious participant can submit harmful updates that the coordinator cannot check against the participant's data, for example to plant a hidden backdoor in the shared model. Defences such as robust aggregation add cost, and the coordinator must also be trusted with the updates it receives.

resources.title: Communication-Efficient Learning of Deep Networks from Decentralized Data
resources.abstract: Modern mobile devices have access to a wealth of data suitable for learning models, which in turn can greatly improve the user experience on the device. For example, language models can improve speech recognition and text entry, and image models can automatically select good photos. However, this rich data is often privacy sensitive, large in quantity, or both, which may preclude logging to the data center and training there using conventional approaches. We advocate an alternative that leaves the training data distributed on the mobile devices, and learns a shared model by aggregating locally-computed updates. We term this decentralized approach Federated Learning. We present a practical method for the federated learning of deep networks based on iterative model averaging, and conduct an extensive empirical evaluation, considering five different model architectures and four datasets. These experiments demonstrate the approach is robust to the unbalanced and non-IID data distributions that are a defining characteristic of this setting. Communication costs are the principal constraint, and we show a reduction in required communication rounds by 10-100x as compared to synchronized stochastic gradient descent.

Federated learning for predicting clinical outcomes in patients with COVID-19
resources.abstract: Federated learning (FL) is a method used for training artificial intelligence models with data from multiple sources while maintaining data anonymity, thus removing many barriers to data sharing. Here we used data from 20 institutes across the globe to train a FL model, called EXAM (electronic medical record (EMR) chest X-ray AI model), that predicts the future oxygen requirements of symptomatic patients with COVID-19 using inputs of vital signs, laboratory data and chest X-rays. EXAM achieved an average area under the curve (AUC) >0.92 for predicting outcomes at 24 and 72 h from the time of initial presentation to the emergency room, and it provided 16% improvement in average AUC measured across all participating sites and an average increase in generalizability of 38% when compared with models trained at a single site using that site's data. For prediction of mechanical ventilation treatment or death at 24 h at the largest independent test site, EXAM achieved a sensitivity of 0.950 and specificity of 0.882. In this study, FL facilitated rapid data science collaboration without data exchange and generated a model that generalized across heterogeneous, unharmonized datasets for prediction of clinical outcomes in patients with COVID-19, setting the stage for the broader use of FL in healthcare.

resources.title: Federated learning enables big data for rare cancer boundary detection
resources.abstract: Although machine learning (ML) has shown promise across disciplines, out-of-sample generalizability is concerning. This is currently addressed by sharing multi-site data, but such centralization is challenging/infeasible to scale due to various limitations. Federated ML (FL) provides an alternative paradigm for accurate and generalizable ML, by only sharing numerical model updates. Here we present the largest FL study to-date, involving data from 71 sites across 6 continents, to generate an automatic tumor boundary detector for the rare disease of glioblastoma, reporting the largest such dataset in the literature ( n = 6, 314). We demonstrate a 33% delineation improvement for the surgically targetable tumor, and 23% for the complete tumor extent, over a publicly trained model. We anticipate our study to: 1) enable more healthcare studies informed by large diverse data, ensuring meaningful results for rare diseases and underrepresented populations, 2) facilitate further analyses for glioblastoma by releasing our consensus model, and 3) demonstrate the FL effectiveness at such scale and task-complexity as a paradigm shift for multi-site collaborations, alleviating the need for data-sharing.

techniques.name: Homomorphic Encryption
techniques.description: Homomorphic encryption lets a server compute on data that stays encrypted, so the server never sees the underlying values. The data owner encrypts the inputs, the server performs the arithmetic directly on the encrypted data, and only the holder of the secret key can decrypt the result. For machine learning, the model is first rewritten using operations the scheme supports, such as additions, multiplications and polynomial approximations of other functions. Exact schemes return the same answer as the unencrypted computation, while approximate schemes, often used for neural networks, return a close one. The guarantee is confidentiality of the data while it is processed, on the usual assumption that the server follows the protocol.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital group wants a cloud service to score patients' readmission risk without the provider seeing patient records. The hospital encrypts the patient features, the cloud evaluates a logistic regression model on the encrypted values, and the hospital decrypts the scores. A linear model is chosen on purpose, since encrypted computation becomes costly as models get larger.

A bank outsources credit scoring to a third-party cloud host. It encrypts customer financial data under a key that never leaves the bank, so an attacker who breaches the host, or an administrator there, can only copy ciphertexts. The bank checks that the host holds no decryption key and that the chosen parameters meet its required security level.

A research team outsources a genome-wide association study to a cloud server. The team encrypts participants' genotype and phenotype data, the server computes the association statistics on the ciphertexts, and only the final statistics are decrypted. One published prototype handled 1,000 individuals and 131,071 genetic variants in about ten minutes on a 28-core server.

limitations.description: Computation is typically orders of magnitude slower than on unencrypted data and ciphertexts are much larger, so real-time use, large models and large datasets are often out of reach. A published encrypted logistic regression training run took about 116 minutes on a real-world dataset.

Only some computations are practical. Circuit depth is limited by noise growth unless costly bootstrapping resets it, and comparisons and non-polynomial functions, such as most neural-network activations, must be approximated or quantised to integers, which can lower accuracy compared with the unencrypted model.

The usual security model is an honest-but-curious server. Ciphertexts can be altered, so encryption alone gives no assurance that the server ran the intended computation correctly, and a malicious host could return a wrong result that still decrypts without error.

Encryption protects data during processing, not what the result reveals. Whoever decrypts the output can still learn about the model or the data behind it through attacks such as membership inference, and with the approximate CKKS scheme, sharing decrypted results can enable a key-recovery attack.

Correct use needs cryptographic expertise. Choosing scheme parameters, encodings and noise budgets wrongly can leave the system insecure or stop results decrypting correctly, and the right choices differ by scheme and library.

resources.title: Fully homomorphic encryption using ideal lattices
resources.abstract: We propose a fully homomorphic encryption scheme -- i.e., a scheme that allows one to evaluate circuits over encrypted data without being able to decrypt. Our solution comes in three steps. First, we provide a general result -- that, to construct an encryption scheme that permits evaluation of arbitrary circuits, it suffices to construct an encryption scheme that can evaluate (slightly augmented versions of) its own decryption circuit; we call a scheme that can evaluate its (augmented) decryption circuit bootstrappable.
