Secure Logistic Regression Based on Homomorphic Encryption: Design and Evaluation
resources.abstract: BACKGROUND: Learning a model without accessing raw data has been an intriguing idea to security and machine learning researchers for years. In an ideal setting, we want to encrypt sensitive data to store them on a commercial cloud and run certain analyses without ever decrypting the data to preserve privacy. Homomorphic encryption technique is a promising candidate for secure data outsourcing, but it is a very challenging task to support real-world machine learning tasks. Existing frameworks can only handle simplified cases with low-degree polynomials such as linear means classifier and linear discriminative analysis. OBJECTIVE: The goal of this study is to provide a practical support to the mainstream learning models (eg, logistic regression). METHODS: We adapted a novel homomorphic encryption scheme optimized for real numbers computation. We devised (1) the least squares approximation of the logistic function for accuracy and efficiency (ie, reduce computation cost) and (2) new packing and parallelization techniques. RESULTS: Using real-world datasets, we evaluated the performance of our model and demonstrated its feasibility in speed and memory consumption. For example, it took approximately 116 minutes to obtain the training model from the homomorphically encrypted Edinburgh dataset. In addition, it gives fairly accurate predictions on the testing dataset. CONCLUSIONS: We present the first homomorphically encrypted logistic regression outsourcing model based on the critical observation that the precision loss of classification models is sufficiently small so that the decision plan stays still.

resources.title: Optimized homomorphic encryption solution for secure genome-wide association studies
resources.abstract: Background Genome-Wide Association Studies (GWAS) refer to observational studies of a genome-wide set of genetic variants across many individuals to see if any genetic variants are associated with a certain trait. A typical GWAS analysis of a disease phenotype involves iterative logistic regression of a case/control phenotype on a single-neuclotide polymorphism (SNP) with quantitative covariates. GWAS have been a highly successful approach for identifying genetic-variant associations with many poorly-understood diseases. However, a major limitation of GWAS is the dependence on individual-level genotype/phenotype data and the corresponding privacy concerns. Methods We present a solution for secure GWAS using homomorphic encryption (HE) that keeps all individual data encrypted throughout the association study. Our solution is based on an optimized semi-parallel GWAS compute model, a new Residue-Number-System (RNS) variant of the Cheon-Kim-Kim-Song (CKKS) HE scheme, novel techniques to switch between data encodings, and more than a dozen crypto-engineering optimizations. Results Our prototype can perform the full GWAS computation for 1,000 individuals, 131,071 SNPs, and 3 covariates in about 10 minutes on a modern server computing node (with 28 cores). Our solution for a smaller dataset was awarded co-first place in iDASH’18 Track 2: “Secure Parallel Genome Wide Association Studies using HE”. Conclusions Many of the HE optimizations presented in our paper are general-purpose, and can be used in solving challenging problems with large datasets in other application domains.

techniques.name: Quantile Regression
techniques.description: Quantile regression predicts chosen percentiles of an outcome, such as the 10th, 50th and 90th, rather than only its average. In the classical method a separate model is fitted for each percentile, using a loss that penalises under-prediction and over-prediction unequally. For example, instead of predicting an average house price of £300,000, it can predict that a house of a given size and location has a 10% chance of selling below £250,000 and a 90% chance of selling below £380,000. Comparing the fitted percentiles shows how features affect different parts of the outcome, such as size mattering more for expensive homes than for cheap ones. A low and a high percentile together give a prediction interval (a range expected to contain a new outcome) without assuming the errors are normally distributed, though how often the interval actually contains new outcomes must be checked on held-out data.

example_use_cases.description: Predicting patient recovery times after surgery by fitting the 10th, 50th and 90th percentiles, so clinicians can say 'most patients recover within 2 to 4 weeks, but one in ten takes longer than 8' when planning follow-up care and bed use.

A grid operator extends its wind power forecast with 10th and 90th percentile forecasts, fitted on past forecast errors and weather conditions, and sizes reserve capacity to the 90th percentile of the next-day shortfall rather than to an average error.

A flood-forecasting agency fits high percentiles of river level on rainfall and soil moisture, giving an upper bound that does not assume symmetric errors, and uses it to decide when to issue warnings for extreme events.

limitations.description: Cost grows with the number of quantile levels fitted when, as in the classical method, each level is a separate optimisation, which adds up on large datasets or with complex models.

May produce crossing quantiles without proper constraints, where predicted 90th percentile values are lower than 50th percentile values, creating logically inconsistent and unusable prediction intervals.

Extreme quantiles (for example the 5th or 95th) rest on few observations and, with heavy-tailed outcomes, are noisy and unstable. With small datasets they cannot be estimated reliably, because too few points lie in the tails.

Gives no guarantee that an interval built from two quantiles contains the stated share of new outcomes. Coverage can fall short if the model form is wrong or the data shift, so check it on held-out data before relying on it.

In its classical form each conditional quantile is assumed to be linear in the features. If the true relationship is curved or has interactions, the fitted quantiles are biased, and flexible models that avoid this lose the readable coefficients.

Using quantile regression to extend an existing wind power forecasting system with probabilistic forecasts
resources.abstract: For operational planning it is important to provide information about the situation‐dependent uncertainty of a wind power forecast. Factors which influence the uncertainty of a wind power forecast include the predictability of the actual meteorological situation, the level of the predicted wind speed (due to the non‐linearity of the power curve) and the forecast horizon. With respect to the predictability of the actual meteorological situation a number of explanatory variables are considered, some inspired by the literature. The article contains an overview of related work within the field. An existing wind power forecasting system (Zephyr/WPPT) is considered and it is shown how analysis of the forecast error can be used to build a model of the quantiles of the forecast error. Only explanatory variables or indices which are predictable are considered, whereby the model obtained can be used for providing situation‐dependent information regarding the uncertainty. Finally, the article contains directions enabling the reader to replicate the methods and thereby extend other forecast systems with situation‐dependent information on uncertainty.

sample_claims.text: The flood forecasting model estimates the specified lower and upper conditional quantiles of river level without imposing a symmetric error distribution, and how often observed levels fall inside them has been checked on held-out events.

The 90th percentile recovery-time forecast exceeds the observed recovery time for at least 90% of patients in the held-out audit sample, so the quoted longest timeframe is not systematically too short.
The wind power forecast's 10th to 90th percentile band contains observed output about 80% of the time on out-of-sample data, in each of the low, medium and high wind-speed ranges.

techniques.name: Temperature Scaling
techniques.description: Temperature scaling is a correction applied after training to a classifier that is more confident than it is accurate, a common problem in modern neural networks. It divides the model's raw scores (logits) by a single number, the temperature, before they are turned into probabilities, so a temperature above one lowers confidence and one below one raises it. The temperature is fitted on a labelled validation set kept apart from training by minimising negative log-likelihood, a measure that penalises confident wrong answers, and the model's own weights are not changed. Because dividing by one positive number never changes which class scores highest, predictions and accuracy stay the same. Stated confidence usually moves much closer to observed accuracy on data like the validation set, which a reliability diagram (a chart of stated confidence against how often the model was right) can show, but some miscalibration remains.

example_use_cases.description: A trust-and-safety team auto-removes posts only when its neural text classifier reports at least 95% confidence. The team fits a temperature on one labelled validation set, then checks on a second, unseen labelled set that posts scored near 95% really are abusive about 95% of the time, and adjusts the removal threshold if they are not.

An environmental agency's land-cover classifier was trained on summer satellite images and is now used on winter scenes, where it is overconfident. The team fits a fresh temperature on a small labelled winter sample and compares calibration error before and after on separate winter test scenes, rather than reusing the summer temperature.

A hospital radiology department displays the model's confidence beside each chest X-ray finding. Before display, the team fits a temperature on held-out scans from its own hospital and reports expected calibration error on a test set, so that clinicians can read a displayed 70% as roughly 70 correct findings in 100 similar cases.

limitations.description: A single temperature is fitted for the whole dataset, so it corrects average overconfidence but not differences between groups or regions of the input space. A minority group can stay overconfident while overall calibration looks good, and only a per-group calibration check shows it.

It leaves predicted classes unchanged, so accuracy and the model's mistakes stay as they were. A weak model remains weak and only becomes more honest about it, so calibration cannot substitute for improving the model.

The temperature is fitted on data resembling the training distribution, and calibration can degrade when deployment data shifts. In one large benchmark, error in stated confidence rose significantly as shift increased, even though it was low on unshifted data.

It needs labelled held-out data that resembles deployment, separate from the training data, and a further separate set to measure the result, because scoring calibration on the data used to fit the temperature flatters it. Small datasets may not leave enough for both.

Calibration is judged on the confidence of the predicted class only. The probabilities given to the other classes are not checked by that measure, so uses that read the whole probability list, such as ranking several likely diagnoses, need separate testing.

resources.title: On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks
resources.abstract: Confidence calibration -- the problem of predicting probability estimates representative of the true correctness likelihood -- is important for classification models in many applications. We discover that modern neural networks, unlike those from a decade ago, are poorly calibrated. Through extensive experiments, we observe that depth, width, weight decay, and Batch Normalization are important factors influencing calibration. We evaluate the performance of various post-processing calibration methods on state-of-the-art architectures with image and document classification datasets. Our analysis and experiments not only offer insights into neural network learning, but also provide a simple and straightforward recipe for practical settings: on most datasets, temperature scaling -- a single-parameter variant of Platt Scaling -- is surprisingly effective at calibrating predictions.

techniques.name: Deep Ensembles
techniques.description: Deep ensembles estimate how uncertain a neural network's predictions are by training several copies of the same network independently and comparing what they predict. Each copy starts from different random initial weights, sees the training data in a different random order, and is trained to output a full predictive distribution, such as a probability for each class or a predicted value with its spread, rather than a single answer. The ensemble's prediction is the average of its members. Where members agree the prediction is usually more reliable, though agreement alone is no guarantee, and where they disagree the model is showing uncertainty about which answer is right, known as epistemic or model uncertainty. In the original study, ensembles of about five networks were better calibrated than single networks, meaning their stated confidence matched how often they were right, and expressed higher uncertainty on inputs from classes absent from the training data.

example_use_cases.description: An autonomous vehicle team runs five independently trained obstacle-detection networks on each camera frame. When the members' outputs disagree beyond a set level, the vehicle slows and requests remote assistance instead of acting on the averaged detection.

A research team estimating body composition from MRI scans trains an ensemble of regression networks that each predict a measurement and its uncertainty, and flags scans where the ensemble is highly uncertain for manual checking before the values enter a population study.

A bank's underwriters see the spread of an ensemble's predicted default probabilities alongside each credit score. Scores with a wide spread are labelled low-confidence and sent for manual review, so staff can see where the model is unsure.

limitations.description: Training and running M networks multiplies compute, memory and latency by roughly M. A five-member ensemble costs about five times a single model, which can rule it out for very large models or for real-time and edge deployment.
Members trained on the same data share its blind spots. On inputs far from the training data they can agree on a confident wrong answer, so low disagreement is not evidence that an input is familiar.

Applies only where the networks can be trained from scratch, with access to the training data and the compute for several full training runs. It cannot be added to an existing pretrained or third-party model.

Disagreement among a small number of members is a noisy estimate, and members that end up too alike understate uncertainty. Calibration has to be checked on held-out data, not assumed from the ensemble.

Uncertainty depends on the training objective and what each member predicts. In regression, variance across member means alone omits the within-member variability included in the original probabilistic method.

resources.title: Simple and Scalable Predictive Uncertainty Estimation using Deep Ensembles
resources.abstract: Deep neural networks (NNs) are powerful black box predictors that have recently achieved impressive performance on a wide spectrum of tasks. Quantifying predictive uncertainty in NNs is a challenging and yet unsolved problem. Bayesian NNs, which learn a distribution over weights, are currently the state-of-the-art for estimating predictive uncertainty; however these require significant modifications to the training procedure and are computationally expensive compared to standard (non-Bayesian) NNs. We propose an alternative to Bayesian NNs that is simple to implement, readily parallelizable, requires very little hyperparameter tuning, and yields high quality predictive uncertainty estimates. Through a series of experiments on classification and regression benchmarks, we demonstrate that our method produces well-calibrated uncertainty estimates which are as good or better than approximate Bayesian NNs. To assess robustness to dataset shift, we evaluate the predictive uncertainty on test examples from known and unknown distributions, and show that our method is able to express higher uncertainty on out-of-distribution examples. We demonstrate the scalability of our method by evaluating predictive uncertainty estimates on ImageNet.

Uncertainty-aware body composition analysis with deep regression ensembles on UK Biobank MRI
resources.abstract: Along with rich health-related metadata, medical images have been acquired for over 40,000 male and female UK Biobank participants, aged 44-82, since 2014. Phenotypes derived from these images, such as measurements of body composition from MRI, can reveal new links between genetics, cardiovascular disease, and metabolic conditions. In this work, six measurements of body composition and adipose tissues were automatically estimated by image-based, deep regression with ResNet50 neural networks from neck-to-knee body MRI. Despite the potential for high speed and accuracy, these networks produce no output segmentations that could indicate the reliability of individual measurements. The presented experiments therefore examine uncertainty quantification with mean-variance regression and ensembling to estimate individual measurement errors and thereby identify potential outliers, anomalies, and other failure cases automatically. In 10-fold cross-validation on data of about 8500 subjects, mean-variance regression and ensembling showed complementary benefits, reducing the mean absolute error across all predictions by 12%. Both improved the calibration of uncertainties and their ability to identify high prediction errors. With intra-class correlation coefficients (ICC) above 0.97, all targets except the liver fat content yielded relative measurement errors below 5%. Testing on another 1000 subjects showed consistent performance, and the method was finally deployed for inference to 30,000 subjects with missing reference values. The results indicate that deep regression ensembles could ultimately provide automated, uncertainty-aware measurements of body composition for more than 120,000 UK Biobank neck-to-knee body MRI that are to be acquired within the coming years.

The ensemble's predicted probabilities are calibrated on held-out data, so that predictions made with 90% confidence are correct about 90% of the time.
When shown inputs from a class absent from the training data, the ensemble's disagreement is measurably higher than on in-distribution inputs, as tested on a held-out set of unseen-class examples.

The driving system reports an uncertainty level with each detection, derived from disagreement between independently trained networks, and remote operators are alerted when it passes the documented limit.
Each credit score shown to underwriters carries an uncertainty range from the ensemble, and scores with a wide range are labelled as low-confidence.

techniques.name: Monotonicity Constraints
techniques.description: Monotonicity constraints require a model's prediction to move only one way as a chosen input rises, with the other inputs held fixed, so that, for example, predicted salary never falls as years of experience increase. The direction for each constrained feature is set from domain knowledge before training, and the learning algorithm or model structure then rules out any fit that breaks it, so the model cannot learn reversals that come from noise or sampling quirks in the data. Boosted-tree libraries apply the constraint when they choose splits and monotonic neural networks build it into their structure, while penalty-based methods only discourage violations. Because a penalty, a constraint set on the wrong column or a later processing step can still let a reversal through, testers then vary each constrained input across its range over many generated or real cases, with the other inputs fixed, and count any prediction that moves the wrong way. The evidence is that violation count, expected to be zero, together with a comparison of held-out accuracy with and without the constraint.

example_use_cases.description: A mortgage lender constrains its approval model so that higher income, longer employment and a higher credit score can only raise the approval score. Loan officers can then tell an applicant that improving any of these factors can only help the application, and the lender can state each factor's direction to its regulator.

A water utility's pipe-burst risk model is constrained so that risk rises with pipe age and operating pressure and falls with the quality of recent maintenance. Asset managers can then explain the ranked inspection list to the regulator through three directional rules, instead of an opaque score.

A hospital analytics team builds a tree-based model that predicts the cost of care for each patient and constrains the prediction never to fall as age or number of chronic conditions rises. Before release they sweep each constrained feature across its range for thousands of generated patient records, with the other features held fixed, and confirm that no prediction moves the wrong way. They also compare held-out accuracy with and without the constraints.

A utility's day-ahead demand forecast for office buildings is constrained so that predicted demand never falls as occupancy or floor area rises. The validation team writes this as an automated test that draws random building profiles, raises one constrained input at a time and fails the build if any forecast drops, so a retrained model that breaks the rule is caught before deployment.

limitations.description: Forces a one-way relationship even where the real one reverses, such as an inverted U between experience and performance. The model then fits that feature worse and cannot show the turning point, so held-out accuracy should be compared with and without the constraint.

Choosing which features to constrain, and in which direction, needs domain expertise. A wrong constraint builds a false belief into the model, and the check on the trained model will still pass, because it shows only that the constraint holds, not that it is right.

The rule covers one feature with the others held fixed, and says nothing about the size of the effect. A model can meet it by ignoring the feature, and when correlated inputs move together a person's overall score can still fall as one favourable input rises, so the constraint does not make the whole model easy to explain.

Support differs by model family. Tree-boosting libraries such as XGBoost accept constraints directly, while neural networks need a special architecture or a penalty term. With histogram-based tree methods, constraints can remove every candidate split and leave shallow trees that underfit.

A sweep or property-based test samples the input space. It can find a violation but cannot prove there is none, and a pass depends on how well the generated inputs cover realistic and rare combinations of features.

resources.abstract: Neural network techniques are widely used in solving pattern recognition or classification problems. However, when statistical data are used in supervised training of a neural network employing the back‐propagation least mean square algorithm, the behavior of the classification boundary during training is often unpredictable. This research suggests the application of monotonicity constraints to the back propagation learning algorithm. When the training sample set is preprocessed by a linear classification function, neural network performance and efficiency can be improved in classification applications where the feature vector is related monotonically to the pattern vector. Since most classification problems in business possess monotonic properties, this technique is useful in those problems where any assumptions about the properties of the data are inappropriate.

resources.title: An informed monotone neural network for multi-stage chronic kidney disease prediction with integrated GFR estimation
resources.abstract: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a progressive condition affecting over 850 million people worldwide, where timely detection and accurate staging are critical to reducing morbidity, mortality, and healthcare burden. Current machine learning approaches often treat CKD prediction as a binary task, neglecting the ordered nature of disease stages, and rarely incorporate physiological constraints or calibrated probability estimates essential for clinical decision support. We propose a multi-stage CKD prediction framework that integrates ordinal classification, probability calibration, and a serum creatinine-monotonicity constraint within a knowledge distillation paradigm. A calibrated CatBoost model serves as a teacher, transferring temperature-scaled class probabilities to an ordinal neural network student augmented with an auxiliary eGFR regression task. Evaluated on a cohort of 750 patients from Al-Ramadi Teaching Hospital, our approach achieved superior macro-F1 and reduced expected calibration error. This work demonstrates that combining ordinal learning, calibration, and physiological constraints yields models that are not only accurate but also aligned with clinical reasoning, offering a pathway toward safer and more trustworthy AI tools for CKD management. Limitations like circular reasoning and target leakage are also discussed.

The clinical risk score is documented as never falling when a vital-sign measure worsens, other measures being equal, and clinicians are given that rule before they use the score.
In property-based testing over generated patient records, raising age or the number of chronic conditions on its own never lowered the cost model's prediction, and the test is rerun on every release
In sweeps of each constrained input across its full range, the building demand forecast recorded no case where predicted demand fell as occupancy rose.
Across 100,000 generated applicant records, raising income alone never lowered the lending model's predicted approval probability.

techniques.name: Generalized Additive Models
techniques.description: A generalised additive model (GAM) builds its prediction by adding a baseline and one smooth curve for each input feature. It extends linear and logistic regression by letting each feature's effect bend, so the model can follow patterns such as risk that climbs steeply after a certain age. Each curve is learned from the data with a smoothing method, such as splines (flexible curves built from joined polynomial pieces). Plotting the curves shows how each feature moves the prediction across its range, so the model can be read directly without a separate explanation method. Because the curves are added together, the model does not capture the joint effect of two features unless a combined term is added by hand.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital builds its 30-day readmission model as a GAM so that its governance committee can audit it. The committee reviews one curve each for age, blood pressure and medication adherence, and queries any stretch where predicted risk falls as a known risk factor rises, since that can point to a data problem rather than a real effect.

A lender uses a GAM for credit scoring so that it can tell a declined applicant how income, credit history and debt-to-income ratio each moved their score. Each factor has its own curve, so the explanation comes straight from the model and needs no separate explanation tool.

An environmental agency models river nitrate levels with a GAM and plots the curve for rainfall. The curve shows the effect levelling off above a certain rainfall, which analysts report to catchment managers instead of a single regression coefficient.

limitations.description: Each feature acts separately, so the model cannot represent effects that depend on two features together, such as the impact of a dose varying with age. Product terms can be added by hand, but each must be thought of in advance and adds a surface that is harder to read than a curve.

The smoothness of each curve is a modelling choice. Cross-validation or penalised fitting selects it automatically, but too little smoothing gives wiggly curves that look like real effects and too much hides genuine bends, so each curve should be read with its confidence band.

When features are strongly related, such as income and age, a nonlinear form of collinearity called concurvity lets one curve absorb part of another's effect. The individual curves can then misstate how much each feature influences the prediction.

A model with dozens of smooth terms produces dozens of curves. Reading them all is slow, so reviewers tend to inspect only the largest effects, and the transparency benefit shrinks as the number of terms grows.
Terms add on the chosen link scale. In a logistic GAM they are contributions to log-odds, not independent additions to readmission probability or guaranteed causal feature effects.

Generalized Additive Models
resources.abstract: Likelihood-based regression models such as the normal linear regression model and the linear logistic model, assume a linear (or some other parametric) form for the covariates X1, X2, …, Xp. We introduce the class of generalized additive models which replaces the linear form Σ βjXj by a sum of smooth functions Σ sj(Xj). The sj(·)'s are unspecified functions that are estimated using a scatterplot smoother, in an iterative procedure we call the local scoring algorithm. The technique is applicable to any likelihood-based regression model: the class of generalized linear models contains many of these. In this class the linear predictor η = Σ βjXj is replaced by the additive predictor Σ sj(Xj); hence, the name generalized additive models. We illustrate the technique with binary response and survival data. In both cases, the method proves to be useful in uncovering nonlinear covariate effects. It has the advantage of being completely automatic, i.e., no "detective work" is needed on the part of the statistician. As a theoretical underpinning, the technique is viewed as an empirical method of maximizing the expected log likelihood, or equivalently, of minimizing the Kullback-Leibler distance to the true model.

resources.title: Fast Stable Restricted Maximum Likelihood and Marginal Likelihood Estimation of Semiparametric Generalized Linear Models
resources.abstract: Recent work by Reiss and Ogden provides a theoretical basis for sometimes preferring restricted maximum likelihood (REML) to generalized cross-validation (GCV) for smoothing parameter selection in semiparametric regression. However, existing REML or marginal likelihood (ML) based methods for semiparametric generalized linear models (GLMs) use iterative REML or ML estimation of the smoothing parameters of working linear approximations to the GLM. Such indirect schemes need not converge and fail to do so in a non-negligible proportion of practical analyses. By contrast, very reliable prediction error criteria smoothing parameter selection methods are available, based on direct optimization of GCV, or related criteria, for the GLM itself. Since such methods directly optimize properly defined functions of the smoothing parameters, they have much more reliable convergence properties. The paper develops the first such method for REML or ML estimation of smoothing parameters. A Laplace approximation is used to obtain an approximate REML or ML for any GLM, which is suitable for efficient direct optimization. This REML or ML criterion requires that Newton–Raphson iteration, rather than Fisher scoring, be used for GLM fitting, and a computationally stable approach to this is proposed. The REML or ML criterion itself is optimized by a Newton method, with the derivatives required obtained by a mixture of implicit differentiation and direct methods. The method will cope with numerical rank deficiency in the fitted model and in fact provides a slight improvement in numerical robustness on the earlier method of Wood for prediction error criteria based smoothness selection. Simulation results suggest that the new REML and ML methods offer some improvement in mean-square error performance relative to GCV or Akaike’s information criterion in most cases, without the small number of severe undersmoothing failures to which Akaike’s information criterion and GCV are prone. This is achieved at the same computational cost as GCV or Akaike’s information criterion. The new approach also eliminates the convergence failures of previous REML- or ML-based approaches for penalized GLMs and usually has lower computational cost than these alternatives. Example applications are presented in adaptive smoothing, scalar on function regression and generalized additive model selection.

Intelligible Models for HealthCare
resources.abstract: In machine learning often a tradeoff must be made between accuracy and intelligibility. More accurate models such as boosted trees, random forests, and neural nets usually are not intelligible, but more intelligible models such as logistic regression, naive-Bayes, and single decision trees often have significantly worse accuracy. This tradeoff sometimes limits the accuracy of models that can be applied in mission-critical applications such as healthcare where being able to understand, validate, edit, and trust a learned model is important. We present two case studies where high-performance generalized additive models with pairwise interactions (GA2Ms) are applied to real healthcare problems yielding intelligible models with state-of-the-art accuracy. In the pneumonia risk prediction case study, the intelligible model uncovers surprising patterns in the data that previously had prevented complex learned models from being fielded in this domain, but because it is intelligible and modular allows these patterns to be recognized and removed. In the 30-day hospital readmission case study, we show that the same methods scale to large datasets containing hundreds of thousands of patients and thousands of attributes while remaining intelligible and providing accuracy comparable to the best (unintelligible) machine learning methods.

sample_claims.text: Every input to the readmission risk model acts through a single plotted curve, so a clinician can read off how predicted risk changes with each input without running a separate explanation method.
The direction of each applicant attribute's effect in the credit model, as plotted with its confidence band, matches what credit risk specialists expect, and any departure has been explained.
The resource allocation model's score for any case is a baseline plus one contribution per policy factor, so each factor's share of a decision can be stated and audited.
Each nonlinear effect the model reports departs from a straight line by more than the width of its confidence band, so the bend is not an artefact of over-flexible smoothing.

techniques.name: Neuron Activation Analysis
techniques.description: Neuron activation analysis examines when individual neurons in a neural network respond strongly. The analyst runs a set of inputs through the model, finds the inputs that activate a chosen neuron most and least, and looks for the concept that separates them, such as buildings in an image classifier or French text in a language model. Some methods test the match automatically, for example by scoring how closely a neuron's activation lines up with labelled examples of a concept. The result is a list of neurons with candidate meanings and the evidence behind each. These meanings are correlations between inputs and activations, so they show what a neuron responds to, not what it does to the model's output.

example_use_cases.description: An ML team inspects a scene classifier trained to sort building and street images. For each neuron in a late layer they compare the images that activate it most with those that do not, using object labels from the dataset. Some neurons line up with a clear concept such as a building and others only weakly, which tells the team how much of the layer can be read.

A hospital assurance team examines a clinical language model and finds neurons whose strongest activations come from text about a particular drug class or condition. A clinician reviews whether the concepts are the expected ones. The finding shows which clinical concepts the model represents internally, not that these neurons cause any particular suggestion.

limitations.description: Many neurons respond to several unrelated concepts, or play different roles depending on the surrounding input. A single label such as 'toxic language' can then be wrong or only part of the story, and consistent interpretation across scenarios is hard.

Behaviour is often spread across many neurons instead of held in one, so a neuron-by-neuron view can miss it. Checking combinations of neurons is much harder than checking single ones, and the number of combinations grows quickly.

The analysis shows which inputs make a neuron fire, not what the neuron contributes to the output. Showing that a neuron matters needs a separate experiment that switches it off or alters it and measures the effect.

A neuron can only be matched to concepts the analyst has examples for. In image models this means a densely labelled dataset, and a neuron whose concept is missing from it goes unexplained or is mislabelled.

The method needs access to the model's internal activations, so it cannot be used on a model reached only through an API. Large language models have hundreds of thousands of neurons or more, so in practice only a chosen subset can be examined and labelled with care.

resources.title: On the Value of Labeled Data and Symbolic Methods for Hidden Neuron Activation Analysis
resources.abstract: A major challenge in Explainable AI is in correctly interpreting activations of hidden neurons: accurate interpretations would help answer the question of what a deep learning system internally detects as relevant in the input, demystifying the otherwise black-box nature of deep learning systems. The state of the art indicates that hidden node activations can, in some cases, be interpretable in a way that makes sense to humans, but systematic automated methods that would be able to hypothesize and verify interpretations of hidden neuron activations are underexplored. This is particularly the case for approaches that can both draw explanations from substantial background knowledge, and that are based on inherently explainable (symbolic) methods.   In this paper, we introduce a novel model-agnostic post-hoc Explainable AI method demonstrating that it provides meaningful interpretations. Our approach is based on using a Wikipedia-derived concept hierarchy with approximately 2 million classes as background knowledge, and utilizes OWL-reasoning-based Concept Induction for explanation generation. Additionally, we explore and compare the capabilities of off-the-shelf pre-trained multimodal-based explainable methods.   Our results indicate that our approach can automatically attach meaningful class expressions as explanations to individual neurons in the dense layer of a Convolutional Neural Network. Evaluation through statistical analysis and degree of concept activation in the hidden layer show that our method provides a competitive edge in both quantitative and qualitative aspects compared to prior work.

resources.title: Network Dissection: Quantifying Interpretability of Deep Visual Representations
resources.abstract: We propose a general framework called Network Dissection for quantifying the interpretability of latent representations of CNNs by evaluating the alignment between individual hidden units and a set of semantic concepts. Given any CNN model, the proposed method draws on a data set of concepts to score the semantics of hidden units at each intermediate convolutional layer. The units with semantics are labeled across a broad range of visual concepts including objects, parts, scenes, textures, materials, and colors. We use the proposed method to test the hypothesis that interpretability is an axis-independent property of the representation space, then we apply the method to compare the latent representations of various networks when trained to solve different classification problems. We further analyze the effect of training iterations, compare networks trained with different initializations, and measure the effect of dropout and batch normalization on the interpretability of deep visual representations. We demonstrate that the proposed method can shed light on characteristics of CNN models and training methods that go beyond measurements of their discriminative power.

Finding Neurons in a Haystack: Case Studies with Sparse Probing
resources.abstract: Despite rapid adoption and deployment of large language models (LLMs), the internal computations of these models remain opaque and poorly understood. In this work, we seek to understand how high-level human-interpretable features are represented within the internal neuron activations of LLMs. We train $k$-sparse linear classifiers (probes) on these internal activations to predict the presence of features in the input; by varying the value of $k$ we study the sparsity of learned representations and how this varies with model scale. With $k=1$, we localize individual neurons which are highly relevant for a particular feature, and perform a number of case studies to illustrate general properties of LLMs. In particular, we show that early layers make use of sparse combinations of neurons to represent many features in superposition, that middle layers have seemingly dedicated neurons to represent higher-level contextual features, and that increasing scale causes representational sparsity to increase on average, but there are multiple types of scaling dynamics. In all, we probe for over 100 unique features comprising 10 different categories in 7 different models spanning 70 million to 6.9 billion parameters.

sample_claims.text: For each sampled neuron in the clinical language model, the concept that best explains its strongest activations is recorded with a match score, and neurons below the agreed score are reported as not interpreted.
The concept labels assigned to the classifier's late-layer neurons hold on held-out images: the labelled neurons activate far more strongly on images of the concept than on images without it.

techniques.name: Causal Mediation Analysis in Language Models
techniques.description: Causal mediation analysis traces which internal components of a language model carry the effect of a change in the input to the output. The analyst makes a controlled change to the input, such as swapping 'nurse' for 'man' in a prompt, and measures how the model's next-word probabilities shift. To find the indirect effect through one component (a single neuron, or an attention head, which is the part of the model that chooses which earlier words to focus on), they feed the model the original input but give that component the value it took on the changed input. To find the direct effect, they feed the changed input but hold that component at its original value. Repeating this across many components shows where in the network a behaviour is carried.

example_use_cases.description: A safety team finds that a language model gives unsafe medical advice when a request is phrased as an instruction rather than a question. They compare outputs for the two phrasings and use mediation analysis to find which attention heads carry most of the shift in the probability of the unsafe reply, so a fix can target those heads and the analysis can be rerun to check it worked.

A research team studying why a language model sometimes gets subject-verb agreement wrong in sentences with an intervening clause changes the number of the subject noun and measures the shift in the verb's probability. Mediation analysis then shows which neurons carry the number information, and whether the same neurons are used across sentence structures.

limitations.description: Needs white-box access and knowledge of the architecture. The analyst must read and overwrite activations at chosen points inside the model, so it cannot be used on a model offered only through an API, and a poorly chosen intervention point can give misleading conclusions.

Conclusions hold for the contrast tested. Swapping 'nurse' for 'man' and tracking one probability ratio tests a single contrast, and a different prompt set or outcome measure can point to different components. Effects also differ between models: larger GPT-2 models showed larger effects, and masked language models matched less well.

Every component and every prompt needs its own forward passes, so testing all the neurons or heads of a large model on many prompts is expensive. Analysts often test a subset or groups of components, which can miss effects elsewhere in the network.

Single-component effects do not simply add up. Vig et al. found that intervening on all neurons together produced an effect far larger than the sum of the single-neuron effects, so ranking components one at a time can understate or misplace where a behaviour is carried.

The split into direct and indirect effects is not guaranteed to be exact. In a non-linear network the total effect need not equal their sum, and Vig et al. report only an approximate match for GPT-2, so the split should be checked rather than assumed.

resources.title: Investigating Gender Bias in Language Models Using Causal Mediation Analysis
resources.abstract: Common methods for interpreting neural models in natural language processing typically examine either their structure or their behavior, but not both. We propose a methodology grounded in the theory of causal mediation analysis for interpreting which parts of a model are causally implicated in its behavior. It enables us to analyze the mechanisms by which information flows from input to output through various model components, known as mediators. We apply this methodology to analyze gender bias in pre-trained Transformer language models. We study the role of individual neurons and attention heads in mediating gender bias across three datasets designed to gauge a model's sensitivity to gender bias. Our mediation analysis reveals that gender bias effects are (i) sparse, concentrated in a small part of the network; (ii) synergistic, amplified or repressed by different components; and (iii) decomposable into effects flowing directly from the input and indirectly through the mediators.

resources.title: Causal Analysis of Syntactic Agreement Mechanisms in Neural Language Models
resources.abstract: Targeted syntactic evaluations have demonstrated the ability of language models to perform subject-verb agreement given difficult contexts. To elucidate the mechanisms by which the models accomplish this behavior, this study applies causal mediation analysis to pre-trained neural language models. We investigate the magnitude of models’ preferences for grammatical inflections, as well as whether neurons process subject-verb agreement similarly across sentences with different syntactic structures. We uncover similarities and differences across architectures and model sizes—notably, that larger models do not necessarily learn stronger preferences. We also observe two distinct mechanisms for producing subject-verb agreement depending on the syntactic structure of the input sentence. Finally, we find that language models rely on similar sets of neurons when given sentences with similar syntactic structure.

techniques.name: Concept Activation Vectors
techniques.description: A concept activation vector (CAV) is a direction inside a neural network that stands for a human idea such as 'stripes'. The analyst supplies example inputs showing the concept and random counter-examples, and trains a simple linear classifier to separate the network's activations (the values a chosen layer produces) for the two sets. The CAV is the direction at right angles to that classifier's dividing boundary, pointing towards the concept examples. Testing with CAVs (TCAV) then reports, for one output class, the share of its inputs whose class score would rise if the activations moved in the concept's direction, and repeating this with many random counter-example sets and applying a significance test guards against a meaningless direction. Concept sets built from examples of a protected characteristic, such as gender or ethnicity, turn the test into a check of whether a class is sensitive to that characteristic, as the original paper demonstrates.

example_use_cases.description: Auditing a medical imaging model to check whether its chest X-ray classifications are sensitive to diagnostic concepts (like 'tumour characteristics') or to irrelevant ones (like 'scanner type' or 'patient positioning'), so the clinical team can judge whether the model relies on medically relevant information.

A team auditing an image classifier used for content tagging builds concept sets from photographs of people of different ethnicities and genders, with random photographs as the comparison, and tests each output class for significant sensitivity to those concepts, as the original paper did. Classes with significant sensitivity to an ethnicity or gender concept are listed for retraining with balanced data; a low score is not taken as clearance.

A developer of a driver-assistance system documents, for a type-approval authority, how its traffic-sign classifier responds to visual concepts. The report gives significance-tested TCAV scores for the 'stop sign' class against concepts such as graffiti, snow cover and low sun glare, so the authority can see what the classifier's predictions are sensitive to.

limitations.description: Requires clearly defined concept examples and non-concept examples, which can be hard to obtain for abstract or subjective concepts. If the examples differ from the random counter-examples in other ways, such as image source or lighting, the CAV mixes those differences in with the concept.

Assumes the concept is represented as a direction that a linear classifier can pick out at the chosen layer. If the concept is not linearly separable there, the CAV is unreliable, so check that the classifier separates the two sets well before reading any scores.

Results depend heavily on which layer is examined, because layers capture different levels of abstraction. A concept can be invisible at one layer and strong at another, so a single-layer result should not be generalised.

The significance test trains hundreds of classifiers per concept and layer (the paper uses about 500), so cost multiplies with the number of concepts and layers tested. FastCAV, a 2025 preprint, reports speed-ups of up to 63.6 times.

Scores are class-level and describe sensitivity, not cause. A TCAV score is the share of a class's inputs whose score rises along the concept direction, so it does not explain an individual decision, and a high score does not show that the concept causes the prediction.

resources.title: FastCAV: Efficient Computation of Concept Activation Vectors for Explaining Deep Neural Networks
resources.abstract: Concepts such as objects, patterns, and shapes are how humans understand the world. Building on this intuition, concept-based explainability methods aim to study representations learned by deep neural networks in relation to human-understandable concepts. Here, Concept Activation Vectors (CAVs) are an important tool and can identify whether a model learned a concept or not. However, the computational cost and time requirements of existing CAV computation pose a significant challenge, particularly in large-scale, high-dimensional architectures. To address this limitation, we introduce FastCAV, a novel approach that accelerates the extraction of CAVs by up to 63.6x (on average 46.4x). We provide a theoretical foundation for our approach and give concrete assumptions under which it is equivalent to established SVM-based methods. Our empirical results demonstrate that CAVs calculated with FastCAV maintain similar performance while being more efficient and stable. In downstream applications, i.e., concept-based explanation methods, we show that FastCAV can act as a replacement leading to equivalent insights. Hence, our approach enables previously infeasible investigations of deep models, which we demonstrate by tracking the evolution of concepts during model training.

resources.title: Interpretability Beyond Feature Attribution: Quantitative Testing with Concept Activation Vectors (TCAV)
resources.abstract: The interpretation of deep learning models is a challenge due to their size, complexity, and often opaque internal state. In addition, many systems, such as image classifiers, operate on low-level features rather than high-level concepts. To address these challenges, we introduce Concept Activation Vectors (CAVs), which provide an interpretation of a neural net’s internal state in terms of human-friendly concepts. The key idea is to view the high-dimensional internal state of a neural net as an aid, not an obstacle. We show how to use CAVs as part of a technique, Testing with CAVs (TCAV), that uses directional derivatives to quantify the degree to which a user-defined concept is important to a classification result–for example, how sensitive a prediction of “zebra” is to the presence of stripes. Using the domain of image classification as a testing ground, we describe how CAVs may be used to explore hypotheses and generate insights for a standard image classification network as well as a medical application.

resources.title: Global and Local Interpretability for Cardiac MRI Classification
resources.abstract: Deep learning methods for classifying medical images have demonstrated impressive accuracy in a wide range of tasks but often these models are hard to interpret, limiting their applicability in clinical practice. In this work we introduce a convolutional neural network model for identifying disease in temporal sequences of cardiac MR segmentations which is interpretable in terms of clinically familiar measurements. The model is based around a variational autoencoder, reducing the input into a low-dimensional latent space in which classification occurs. We then use the recently developed `concept activation vector' technique to associate concepts which are diagnostically meaningful (eg. clinical biomarkers such as `low left-ventricular ejection fraction') to certain vectors in the latent space. These concepts are then qualitatively inspected by observing the change in the image domain resulting from interpolations in the latent space in the direction of these vectors. As a result, when the model classifies images it is also capable of providing naturally interpretable concepts relevant to that classification and demonstrating the meaning of those concepts in the image domain. Our approach is demonstrated on the UK Biobank cardiac MRI dataset where we detect the presence of coronary artery disease.

resources.title: Concept attribution: Explaining CNN decisions to physicians
resources.abstract: Deep learning explainability is often reached by gradient-based approaches that attribute the network output to perturbations of the input pixels. However, the relevance of input pixels may be difficult to relate to relevant image features in some applications, e.g. diagnostic measures in medical imaging. The framework described in this paper shifts the attribution focus from pixel values to user-defined concepts. By checking if certain diagnostic measures are present in the learned representations, experts can explain and entrust the network output. Being post-hoc, our method does not alter the network training and can be easily plugged into the latest state-of-the-art convolutional networks. This paper presents the main components of the framework for attribution to concepts, in addition to the introduction of a spatial pooling operation on top of the feature maps to obtain a solid interpretability analysis. Furthermore, regularized regression is analyzed as a solution to the regression overfitting in high-dimensionality latent spaces. The versatility of the proposed approach is shown by experiments on two medical applications, namely histopathology and retinopathy, and on one non-medical task, the task of handwritten digit classification. The obtained explanations are in line with clinicians' guidelines and complementary to widely used visualization tools such as saliency maps.

sample_claims.text: The chest X-ray classifier's 'pneumonia' predictions are significantly sensitive to clinically recognised findings and not significantly sensitive to scanner type or patient positioning, at the layers tested.

The content-tagging classifier's TCAV scores for the ethnicity and gender concept sets are recorded for every output class at the tested layers, and the classes with significant sensitivity are listed for review.
The traffic-sign classifier's sensitivity to graffiti, snow cover and glare concepts is documented with significance-tested TCAV scores for each sign class the approval authority has requested.
The object recogniser's class predictions depend mainly on concepts that domain experts regard as meaningful for that class, such as shape and texture, rather than on background concepts.

techniques.name: Fairness GAN
techniques.description: Fairness GAN is a pre-processing method that generates a synthetic training dataset in which decisions no longer track a protected attribute such as gender or skin tone. A generative adversarial network (GAN) is a pair of networks trained against each other, one producing fake examples and one trying to tell them from real ones. Here the generator is conditioned on the protected attribute and produces both an example and its decision label, such as hired or rejected (images in the original work, table rows in Xu et al.'s separate FairGAN). An extra network tries to predict the protected attribute from the generated output, and the generator is rewarded for defeating it, so favourable decisions become more similar across groups. The user can aim for demographic parity, meaning equal rates of favourable decisions, or for equality of opportunity, which applies the constraint only to favourable decisions.

example_use_cases.description: A recruitment technology team holds interview-video stills labelled with past shortlisting decisions that favoured one gender. It trains a Fairness GAN to generate a synthetic image set whose shortlisting labels are similar for women and men, trains the screening model on that set, and compares shortlisting rates by gender on held-out real images before deployment.

A lender's data science team has ten years of loan decisions in which women were approved less often than men on similar incomes. It trains a tabular FairGAN-style generator to produce a synthetic dataset, confirms that the gap in approval rates in the synthetic data is close to zero, and trains its scoring model on that data, testing accuracy and approval rates on real held-out applications.

limitations.description: GAN training is unstable and the fairness loss adds a further pull on the generator. The original authors used spectral normalisation, softened outcome values and added noise to keep training stable, and results still varied across datasets. Expect tuning effort and repeated runs.

Fairness and accuracy trade off, and the gain is uneven. In the original experiments a classifier trained on debiased CelebA data went from about 20 to about 29 per cent error. Demographic parity improved on three of four datasets but not on Quick, Draw!, and the demographic-parity version made equality of opportunity worse on the soccer data.

It needs a lot of data. The authors had only 1,501 labelled soccer images, so they borrowed more than 200,000 unlabelled CelebA faces to help the generator, which is possible only when a large related set exists.

The original method covers a narrow setting: image inputs, one binary protected attribute and a binary outcome, with demographic parity or equality of opportunity but not equalised odds. Continuous protected attributes and non-image data are left as future work, and tabular versions such as FairGAN are separate methods with their own evidence.

Fairness is judged by training a classifier on the synthetic data and testing it on real data, and image quality is judged mainly by inspecting average faces. The authors report that debiasing visibly changes images in stereotyped ways, such as male faces taking on features coded as feminine, so the synthetic data need checking for distortions that the classifier test would miss.

Fairness GAN
resources.abstract: In this paper, we introduce the Fairness GAN, an approach for generating a dataset that is plausibly similar to a given multimedia dataset, but is more fair with respect to protected attributes in allocative decision making. We propose a novel auxiliary classifier GAN that strives for demographic parity or equality of opportunity and show empirical results on several datasets, including the CelebFaces Attributes (CelebA) dataset, the Quick, Draw!\ dataset, and a dataset of soccer player images and the offenses they were called for. The proposed formulation is well-suited to absorbing unlabeled data; we leverage this to augment the soccer dataset with the much larger CelebA dataset. The methodology tends to improve demographic parity and equality of opportunity while generating plausible images.

resources.title: FairGAN: Fairness-aware Generative Adversarial Networks
resources.abstract: Fairness-aware learning is increasingly important in data mining. Discrimination prevention aims to prevent discrimination in the training data before it is used to conduct predictive analysis. In this paper, we focus on fair data generation that ensures the generated data is discrimination free. Inspired by generative adversarial networks (GAN), we present fairness-aware generative adversarial networks, called FairGAN, which are able to learn a generator producing fair data and also preserving good data utility. Compared with the naive fair data generation models, FairGAN further ensures the classifiers which are trained on generated data can achieve fair classification on real data. Experiments on a real dataset show the effectiveness of FairGAN.

resources.title: Bt-GAN: Generating Fair Synthetic Healthdata via Bias-transforming Generative Adversarial Networks
resources.abstract: Synthetic data generation offers a promising solution to enhance the usefulness of Electronic Healthcare Records (EHR) by generating realistic de-identified data. However, the existing literature primarily focuses on the quality of synthetic health data, neglecting the crucial aspect of fairness in downstream predictions. Consequently, models trained on synthetic EHR have faced criticism for producing biased outcomes in target tasks. These biases can arise from either spurious correlations between features or the failure of models to accurately represent sub-groups. To address these concerns, we present Bias-transforming Generative Adversarial Networks (Bt-GAN), a GAN-based synthetic data generator specifically designed for the healthcare domain. In order to tackle spurious correlations (i), we propose an information-constrained Data Generation Process (DGP) that enables the generator to learn a fair deterministic transformation based on a well-defined notion of algorithmic fairness. To overcome the challenge of capturing exact sub-group representations (ii), we incentivize the generator to preserve sub-group densities through score-based weighted sampling. This approach compels the generator to learn from underrepresented regions of the data manifold. To evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed method, we conduct extensive experiments using the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care (MIMIC-III) database. Our results demonstrate that Bt-GAN achieves state-of-the-art accuracy while significantly improving fairness and minimizing bias amplification. Furthermore, we perform an in-depth explainability analysis to provide additional evidence supporting the validity of our study. In conclusion, our research introduces a novel and professional approach to addressing the limitations of synthetic data generation in the healthcare domain. By incorporating fairness considerations and leveraging advanced techniques such as GANs, we pave the way for more reliable and unbiased predictions in healthcare applications.

resources.title: FairFinGAN: Fairness-Aware Synthetic Financial Data Generation
resources.abstract: Financial datasets often suffer from bias that can lead to unfair decision-making in automated systems. In this work, we propose FairFinGAN, a WGAN-based framework designed to generate synthetic financial data while mitigating bias with respect to the protected attribute. Our approach incorporates fairness constraints directly into the training process through a classifier, ensuring that the synthetic data is both fair and preserves utility for downstream predictive tasks. We evaluate our proposed model on five real-world financial datasets and compare it with existing GAN-based data generation methods. Experimental results show that our approach achieves superior fairness metrics without significant loss in data utility, demonstrating its potential as a tool for bias-aware data generation in financial applications.

sample_claims.text: In the synthetic training set generated for the screening model, the rate of favourable shortlisting decisions for women and men differs by less than the tolerance set in the project's fairness requirement.
A credit scoring model trained on the synthetic loan data shows a smaller gap in approval rates between women and men, on held-out real applications, than a model trained on the original data.
The synthetic data remain close enough to the original for the model's purpose: the accuracy cost of training on them, compared with the original data, was measured and judged acceptable.

techniques.name: Prejudice Remover Regulariser
techniques.description: The Prejudice Remover Regulariser, proposed by Kamishima and colleagues (2012), trains a classifier with an extra fairness penalty that discourages its predictions from carrying information about a sensitive attribute such as gender or race. The penalty approximates the 'mutual information' between the predicted label and the sensitive attribute, which measures how much knowing one tells you about the other. It is added to the usual training objective, so the model is pushed to fit the labels while keeping that dependence low. The authors built it into logistic regression and describe it as applicable to other classifiers that output probabilities. One parameter sets the penalty strength, so a practitioner can trade some accuracy for a smaller dependence on the sensitive attribute.

example_use_cases.description: A lender's modelling team retrains its logistic-regression credit-scoring model with the prejudice remover penalty, using applicant gender as the sensitive attribute. It tries several penalty strengths and records how far approval decisions still depend on gender and how much predictive accuracy is lost at each, so the credit committee can choose the strength it will accept.

A health-system analytics team building a postpartum depression risk model on insurance claims trains it with the penalty, with race as the sensitive attribute. It compares disparate impact and equal opportunity difference with an unpenalised model on the same held-out data, to decide whether the penalised model is good enough or another bias-reduction method is needed.

A university building a model to flag students for early support trains it with the penalty so that flags depend less on gender. The team reports to the student-support board how much accuracy the chosen strength costs, and how far the difference in flag rates between genders shrinks, before the model is used.

limitations.description: The penalty strength has to be tuned, and no setting is right in advance. In the original experiments on census income data, the strongest penalty tested cut the difference in positive-prediction rates between men and women from 0.19 to 0.01, but accuracy fell from about 85% to 77%. The choice is a judgement about how much accuracy to give up.

The sensitive attribute is an input to the model at training and at prediction time, in the original method and in the AIF360 implementation. The technique cannot be used where the attribute is not collected or cannot be used when decisions are made.

The penalty measures only how much predictions depend on the sensitive attribute, not whether errors fall evenly across groups. Where groups really differ in outcome rates in the data, pushing the dependence down misclassifies some individuals to meet the target, and no equal-error-rate guarantee follows.

The original method and the AIF360 implementation cover logistic regression only. Using the penalty with a neural network or another model means deriving and implementing it yourself, and the optimisation was designed for the logistic form.

Reduced dependence is measured on the training sample. With little data, the model can depend on the sensitive attribute more on new cases than on the training data, which the original paper calls underestimation, so the dependence should be re-measured on held-out data.

Fairness in credit scoring: Assessment, implementation and profit implications
resources.abstract: The rise of algorithmic decision-making has spawned much research on fair machine learning (ML). Financial institutions use ML for building risk scorecards that support a range of credit-related decisions. Yet, the literature on fair ML in credit scoring is scarce. The paper makes three contributions. First, we revisit statistical fairness criteria and examine their adequacy for credit scoring. Second, we catalog algorithmic options for incorporating fairness goals in the ML model development pipeline. Last, we empirically compare different fairness processors in a profit-oriented credit scoring context using real-world data. The empirical results substantiate the evaluation of fairness measures, identify suitable options to implement fair credit scoring, and clarify the profit-fairness trade-off in lending decisions. We find that multiple fairness criteria can be approximately satisfied at once and recommend separation as a proper criterion for measuring the fairness of a scorecard. We also find fair in-processors to deliver a good balance between profit and fairness and show that algorithmic discrimination can be reduced to a reasonable level at a relatively low cost. The codes corresponding to the paper are available on GitHub.

resources.title: Evaluating Fairness Strategies in Educational Data Mining: A Comparative Study of Bias Mitigation Techniques
resources.abstract: Ensuring fairness in machine learning models applied to educational data is crucial for mitigating biases that can reinforce systemic inequities. This paper compares various fairness-enhancing algorithms across preprocessing, in-processing, and post-processing stages. Preprocessing methods such as Reweighting, Learning Fair Representations, and Disparate Impact Remover aim to adjust training data to reduce bias before model learning. In-processing techniques, including Adversarial Debiasing and Prejudice Remover, intervene during model training to directly minimize discrimination. Post-processing approaches, such as Equalized Odds Post-Processing, Calibrated Equalized Odds Post-Processing, and Reject Option Classification, adjust model predictions to improve fairness without altering the underlying model. We evaluate these methods on educational datasets, examining their effectiveness in reducing disparate impact while maintaining predictive performance. Our findings highlight tradeoffs between fairness and accuracy, as well as the suitability of different techniques for various educational applications.

sample_claims.text: On held-out applications, the mutual information between the credit model's approval decisions and applicant gender is lower than for an otherwise identical unpenalised model, at a penalty strength chosen with its accuracy cost documented.
The gap in shortlisting rates between men and women on held-out data is below the agreed tolerance, with the penalty strength and the accuracy given up at that setting reported.
The postpartum depression risk model's disparate impact ratio between racial groups is closer to 1 than that of the unpenalised model on the same held-out data.

The student-support flagging model's flag rates differ less between genders than those of the unpenalised baseline on held-out students, and the accuracy lost is reported to the student-support board.

techniques.name: Exponentiated Gradient Reduction
techniques.description: Exponentiated gradient reduction trains a classifier that satisfies a chosen fairness criterion, such as demographic parity (equal rates of favourable outcomes across groups) or equalised odds (equal error rates across groups), while keeping error as low as it can. It reduces the problem to a series of ordinary training runs on the same data, each with different example weights. Between runs, a multiplicative update, the exponentiated gradient step, increases the weight on fairness constraints that are currently violated, and a standard classifier is retrained on the reweighted data. The output is a randomised classifier, a weighted mix of the classifiers trained along the way, with one drawn at random for each prediction. The original paper proves that its error and its fairness violation come close to the best achievable, up to a tolerance the user sets and the statistical error from a finite training set.

example_use_cases.description: A recruitment team trains a shortlisting model under a demographic parity constraint so that selection rates are equal across gender groups, and sweeps the method's tolerance setting to see how much accuracy each step towards equality costs.

A justice agency building a recidivism risk model trains a logistic regression under a demographic parity constraint on race, then compares accuracy and fairness metrics against the unconstrained model on the same data before deciding whether to deploy it.

A lender trying equalised odds, true-positive-rate difference and demographic parity as constraints on its credit-scoring model picks the one that gives the best balance of accuracy and profit on its own data, since the best choice differs between datasets.

limitations.description: The guarantees assume the base learner can solve each weighted training problem close to exactly. Real learners only approximate this, so the stated bounds on error and fairness violation are approximate in practice. The learner must also accept per-example weights, which rules out some model types.

The result is a randomised mix of classifiers, so the same input can receive different predictions on repeat requests. This is hard to defend where decisions must be repeatable, as in appeals or audits.

Needs the protected attribute for every training example, although not at prediction time. It enforces one fairness criterion at a time, and the original paper leaves trading off several criteria as an open problem.

Each round retrains the base model, and the number of rounds needed grows with the square of the inverse of the tolerance, so halving the tolerance roughly quadruples training cost. Large datasets or slow models make tight tolerances expensive.

Constraint violation is controlled only up to sampling error, which is larger for small groups. In one credit-scoring comparison the best-performing constraint differed between datasets, so the right criterion has to be found by experiment on the data in hand.

resources.title: A Reductions Approach to Fair Classification
resources.abstract: We present a systematic approach for achieving fairness in a binary classification setting. While we focus on two well-known quantitative definitions of fairness, our approach encompasses many other previously studied definitions as special cases. The key idea is to reduce fair classification to a sequence of cost-sensitive classification problems, whose solutions yield a randomized classifier with the lowest (empirical) error subject to the desired constraints. We introduce two reductions that work for any representation of the cost-sensitive classifier and compare favorably to prior baselines on a variety of data sets, while overcoming several of their disadvantages.
